CHAIR ( Senator Darmanin ): I declare open this hearing of the Economics Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 budget estimates. I begin my acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and paying my respects to their elders past and present, and I extend that respect to any Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. The committee is due to report to the Senate on Tuesday 23 June 2026. The committee has set 12 June 2026 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and 24 July 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will be starting with Treasury, and it is the Macroeconomic Group.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the department and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purposes of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of the department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect.

Department of the Treasury

[09:06]

CHAIR: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Katy Gallagher, Minister for Finance, representing the Treasurer. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Senator Gallagher: No, just my apologies for being held up a little bit.

CHAIR: I welcome the secretary of the Australian Treasury, Jenny Wilkinson, and officers from the Department of the Treasury Macroeconomic Group and International, Corporate and Investment Group. Secretary, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Ms Wilkinson : I do. Thank you, Chair, and thank you to the committee for the opportunity to make this opening statement. I will focus my remarks on macroeconomic developments, particularly new information since the Treasurer delivered the federal budget on 12 May. As you're aware, I delivered an address to the Australian Business Economists last week that traversed a broader set of issues around the budget, and I'm happy to address any questions flowing from that address.

The conflict in the Middle East continues to create a significant negative global supply shock. There are now clear signs that disruptions to the production and trade of oil, liquefied natural gas and petrochemicals are pushing up global inflation and will challenge the outlook for global growth in 2026. Our assessment is that some of Australia's largest trading partners, such as China, Japan and Korea, possess large energy stockpiles and are relatively better positioned to navigate oil and fuel shortages. However, other South-East Asian economies with lower energy reserves and slimmer fiscal buffers are vulnerable to shortfalls, with many already imposing measures to manage energy demand.

Although central banks in many advanced economies have indicated that they will look through the direct inflationary impact of higher oil prices, recent communications confirm they will be concerned about persistent indirect price effects feeding through to core inflation measures. The impacts of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have been cushioned to some extent by a drawdown of global inventories, but there are limits on the extent to which stocks can continue to be drawn down at current rates before operational stress levels increase. This also creates the risk of higher prices in the future if the current disruption continues, even if it doesn't escalate.

Turning to the domestic economy, yesterday's release of the national accounts shows that the Australian economy grew by 0.3 per cent in the March quarter and by 2.5 per cent through the year. This solid result aligns broadly with our expectations at the time of finalising the budget, although the composition of growth varied a bit from our expectations. Growth in the quarter was driven almost entirely by new private demand, particularly new private business investment, which grew by 5.7 per cent in the quarter, reflecting strong investment in data centres. Dwelling investment grew for the ninth consecutive quarter. Adverse weather across the quarter, from cyclones Narelle, Koji and Mitchell impacted commodity exports, while government consumption and household discretionary consumption was subdued.

The March quarter outcome captures only the effects of the first month of the Middle East conflict. The full impact of the conflict will become clearer as we go forward. These will depend on a range of factors, including the duration and severity of the conflict and how businesses, households and governments respond. Treasury's monitoring the situation closely to assess the unfolding effects of the conflict on core measures of inflation and on domestic activity. There's increasing volatility emerging in some data, which in part reflects short-term behavioural changes over the first two months of the conflict. It means it remains too early to tell the longer term effects on outcomes.

The ABS's Monthly Household Spending Indicator showed a 1.1 per cent fall in nominal household spending in April. This was underpinned by a 4.7 per cent fall in transport spending, particularly air transport, as travellers chose to refund or rebook trips in response to the Middle East conflict. Food spending was also down, but this reflected an unwinding of a spike in purchases in March. Spending on discretionary goods weakened in the month.

On the business side, the ABS's latest capital expenditure release reported that businesses have upgraded their capital expenditure intentions for 2025-26, suggesting a rise of 9.1 per cent over the year, up from 3.8 per cent in 2024-25. This strong result is primarily driven by investment by large businesses in data centres and is consistent with the strength in business investment recorded in the March quarter. The ABS has recently reinstated its Business Conditions and Sentiment release to gauge how businesses are managing the impacts of the Middle East conflict. The May survey reported that about two-thirds of businesses were making changes in response to fuel supply and prices. This included absorbing cost increases or delaying and cancelling investment. Smaller businesses appear to have been more heavily impacted. Small and medium businesses reported being more than twice as likely to face difficulties meeting upcoming financial commitments compared to larger businesses. To date, these impacts have not materialised through financial channels. Bank data suggests that business distress levels have remained broadly stable. Indicators such as overdraft utilisation and hardship applications have stabilised at levels similar to those recorded before the conflict.

In light of the current challenges, the budget forecasts that the growth of the Australian economy would ease to 1¾ per cent in 2026-27, and data received over the past month is consistent with that outcome. The effect of the Middle East conflict on both activity and business confidence is expected to weigh on employment growth over the period ahead. In April, employment fell, and the unemployment rate increased to 4½ per cent. However, monthly labour force data can be noisy, and, despite the fall in employment, total hours worked increased, and underemployment fell timely. Timely indicators of labour demands, such as job advertisements, vacancies and survey measures of employment intentions, have softened through April but do not point to a sharp deterioration in labour market conditions. They remain consistent with the unemployment rate remaining below prepandemic levels. The budget forecasts the unemployment rate to stabilise around 4½ per cent, which remains low by historical standards.

Wage growth has also remained broadly steady, consistent with unemployment near its sustainable rate. The wage price index increased by 0.8 per cent in the March quarter to be 3.3 per cent higher through the year. The budget forecasts a slight pick-up in wage growth over the coming year due to increased employee wage claims stemming from the recent increases in inflation and recent Fair Work Commission decisions, including the outcome of the Annual wage review, the phasing out of junior pay rates for workers over the age of 18 and the gender undervaluation determination.

The budget noted that the conflict in the Middle East caused a sharp increase in automotive fuel prices, driving a pick-up in inflation in March. Inflation moderated to 4.2 per cent through the year to April, largely due to some moderation in fuel prices. This reflected the combined impact of the temporary reduction in fuel excise and lower fuel import prices, as regional refiners were able to adjust to disruption from the conflict. There was also some slight easing in some parts of the basket that had been experiencing elevated inflation prior to the conflict, including rents and some food items. Market services inflation, which has also been elevated, remained steady. However, the April inflation data did show some broadening in price pressures from the Middle East conflict. There were strong increases in the price of newly constructed dwellings, as well as freight and logistics. The pass-through of price pressures to consumers is expected to continue in coming months, with food, air travel and construction prices likely to be affected. This is likely to impact both headline and underlying inflation. The budget forecasts headline inflation to peak at around 5 per cent through the year to the June quarter. The budget forecasts inflation to moderate significantly in early 2027. However, the timing of the moderation will depend on the duration of the disruption to oil and broader petrochemical supply chains.

In closing, as highlighted in the budget documents, the Middle East conflict looms large over our outlook for the economy. There remains considerable uncertainty that is yet to resolve. On one other matter, since the last estimates meeting, Dr Guy Debelle has completed his independent review of the Australian Office of Financial Management's operations, and that's available on the Treasury website. It confirmed the AOFM is performing its functions effectively and is highly regarded by market participants. Treasury and the AOFM support the direction set out by the review and are working together to implement the review's recommendations. A more detailed response will be made public in coming weeks. Thank you for the opportunity to give this opening statement, and I welcome your questions.

CHAIR: Thank you very much, Ms Wilkinson. We will throw to questions, but there's significant interest today. I'm going to say to senators at the outset that I'm going to move around in 10-minute blocks. I'll give everyone a warning at eight minutes that you've got two to go. Hopefully that means we'll run smoothly and everyone will get a chance to ask all the questions they need. I'm going to start with Senator Walker.

Senator WALKER: Ms Wilkinson, the budget papers set out the need for tax reform as being driven by a number of factors across intergenerational equity, the differential tax treatment of assets and Australia's long-running productivity challenge. Can you expand on your assessment of these challenges and why tax reform is an urgent priority for the government?

Ms Wilkinson : You're absolutely right that the budget papers set out the case for tax reform and explain in some detail the reforms that the government was announcing in the budget, both on tax and on a range of broader issues. That was articulated in detail in budget statement 4, which goes through, for both, the changes to personal income taxes, the changes to business taxes and then the changes which improve the simplification of the tax system. At the outset of budget statement 4 there are a few issues that are raised which are, if you like, the policy issues that I would suggest were front of mind for government in considering the reforms that they wanted to pursue in the budget.

In relation to intergenerational equity, there are really three sets of issues which are raised and explained in budget statement 4. One of them is the longstanding decline in homeownership rates, which has been discussed in this committee over time and, I think, is widely understood across the community. This has been a long-running trend. The second issue that's raised in terms of a policy challenge is the pressure within the tax system on personal income taxes going forward, in terms of the pressure within the system to use personal income taxes as part of revenue raising to fund government budgets.

The third set of issues that's raised in budget statement 4 is around what the concentration of the benefits of the current concessions is across different parts of the population. In doing that work, Treasury has drawn upon what we now have available to us, which are longitudinal datasets that have enabled us to provide an assessment of what the total benefit of current concessions are by lifetime-income percentiles. That demonstrates that the most significant proportion of the concessions benefit those individuals in the top one per cent of the lifetime-income deciles. Those are the three policy issues that are presented in budget statement 4, and they all go to different ways of thinking about questions of intergenerational equity. In the address that I provided last week, I talked about the fact that, when we think about equity—you can think about intergenerational equity, you can think about horizontal equity, you can think about vertical equity, and all of these are different ways that different people can come at this question.

The second set of issues that is examined in budget statement 4 goes to the question about whether the current capital gains tax arrangements, putting aside a view that one may have about their generosity or otherwise, and whether they do a particularly effective job of adjusting for what's widely regarded as an important adjustment in terms of taxing capital gains on realisation—that is, how effectively they deal with inflation over time and across different assets. There's quite a lot of analysis in there that shows, across different types of assets and across time, that the 50 per cent discount sometimes overcompensates for inflation and sometimes undercompensates for inflation. By doing that, it raises the question about whether that's the most appropriate way of taxing capital gains and adjusting for inflation in order have the tax system have as minimal an impact as possible on decisions that individuals are taking on, say, investment decisions in the economy. That's the second set of issues that are raised.

The third set of issues that are raised in budget statement 4 go to, again, a conversation that we've had at length in this committee around productivity and around: what are the sorts of things that governments should be doing in order to try and support and encourage productivity growth? There, the government, first of all, is open, as it has been, about the productivity challenge, which has been with us for some time and has led them to consider some of the more targeted ways in the tax system that innovative activities can be supported, complemented by a range of other things which were announced in the budget to improve productivity growth.

Senator WALKER: As you'd be aware, house prices have risen about twice as fast as incomes over the past two decades. I note that you already touched on this a little bit, but can you talk us through how some of the budget measures—like changes to negative gearing and capital gains—are going to help level the playing field, especially for young people trying to get into the housing market?

Ms Wilkinson : Again, these issues are covered in budget statement 4. In particular, box 4.4 provides an overarching assessment of the housing measures in the budget. I guess I would just draw out a couple of things. First of all—again, we've had this discussion at length in this committee—supply measures are really important in addressing housing issues in Australia. I think the government has been very clear about that. And, when we think about supply measures, the sorts of things that governments can do and have done include all of the investments that have been made in enabling infrastructure and also the efforts to work with states and territories to improve timelines for things like approvals and to improve planning and zoning arrangements. The other thing is the work that we're doing on the National Construction Code. So there are lots of things that need to be done on the supply side.

Tax measures can have an impact on supply. In particular, our assessment is that the tax measures which were announced in the budget will encourage investors who wish to invest in housing to invest in new housing as opposed to investing in existing dwellings. Also, as box 4.4 outlines, our expectation is that, probably, one of the more significant impacts of the tax changes will be to shift the ownership structure of housing away from investors, to some degree, towards owner-occupiers. And we've done our best modelling in order to try and estimate what the order-of-magnitude impacts of those shifts could be.

CHAIR: You're almost at time, so I'm going to rotate the call.

Senator WALKER: Yes.

CHAIR: Senator Chandler.

Senator CHANDLER: Thank you, everyone, for appearing today. First of all, I did want to flag, Secretary, our thanks for your response to the letter from myself and the deputy chair in relation to some information for the committee. Chair, if I may pass both my letter to the secretary and the secretary's letter to me for consideration for tabling, that would be appreciated. We'll ask some questions about that later on but not first up.

CHAIR: I'm happy to table both of these along with their opening statement.

Senator CHANDLER: Wonderful, thank you. Secretary, will the new capital gains tax system allow five-year income averaging, as the pre-1999 system did?

Ms Wilkinson : That has not been part of the announcements that the government has made in relation to the tax package. So that's a no. That was not announced.

Senator CHANDLER: Did the pre-1999 system impose a minimum 30 per cent tax rate, as the new system will?

Ms Wilkinson : No, it didn't.

Senator CHANDLER: On 19 May, in relation to the CGT changes, which he'd promised more than 50 times before the election not to introduce, the Prime Minister said:

Our policies are very clear: when it comes to capital gains tax, what we are simply doing is returning the system to what was there before 1999.

Is that an accurate statement, Secretary?

Senator Gallagher: I think the PM's comments there were relating to the indexation model/approach that was there in 1999.

Senator CHANDLER: There was no reference to the indexation model in the quote that I just read out.

Senator Gallagher: I don't know what you're drawing from there, but all of my understanding of the comments that have been made about reverting back is around how you, essentially, adjust for indexation and not have a flat 50 per cent deduction.

Senator CHANDLER: 'What we are simply doing is returning the CGT system to what was there before 1999.' That's not accurate, is it?

Senator Gallagher: Again—my previous answer stands there. It relates to the reintroduction of adjusting for indexation.

Senator CHANDLER: My understanding is that the Prime Minister repeated this reference in the parliament last week. I think it was on 26 May. He restated this comment in the parliament. Will he seek to correct the record in that regard? He said:

We are also changing the capital gains tax regime to go back to 1999.

That seems pretty clear cut.

Senator Gallagher: I've answered your question. I know what the Prime Minister's comments related to, and that was that, instead of having the changes that were introduced by Prime Minister Howard to have a 50 per cent deduction for capital gains, we are reverting to the model that existed before that, which is to, essentially, adjust for indexation and tax real gains.

Senator CHANDLER: There was no reference to any of that context, Minister, in the statement that the Prime Minister made in the House last week.

Senator Gallagher: I don't have all the transcripts that you're reading from. But the government has been very clear, when making statements like that, that it's relating to how you treat gains, as opposed to the changes that were brought in by Prime Minister Howard, and reverting back to the system that existed before that in adjusting for indexation and then taxing real gains.

Senator CHANDLER: Minister, you provided a lot of context around this statement, but do you think the Prime Minister understands what he's talking about?

Senator Gallagher: It's a bit early to start the patronising. We've got a long day ahead of us. The Prime Minister has been clear about the changes that we have brought in. He's been clear about why we're making those changes, and they've all been outlined in the budget papers.

Senator CHANDLER: Many young Australians won't remember the pre-1999 system, so I want to ask some questions on their behalf. Under the tax changes that have been proposed, will young Australians have higher taxes imposed on them than previous generations, Secretary?

Ms Wilkinson : I went to this analysis in the speech that I presented last week. I provided some analysis in that speech. Chart 11 in that speech shows what our best estimate is of the combined benefits of the tax reforms—these are the changes to capital gains tax, negative gearing and trusts and then the introduction of the working Australians tax offset and the introduction of the instant deduction—and what impact they would have across different cohorts of young people. In order to do this analysis, you do have to look over a period of time, rather than just looking at a particular point in time, to assess what the benefits are for young people. That analysis shows that around 90 per cent of young people will face lower taxes as a consequence of these changes. That analysis is provided in that paper.

Senator CHANDLER: Will young Australians be paying more tax on investments they are making to save for their first home, Secretary?

Ms Wilkinson : I'm not sure—

Senator Gallagher: I think it's pretty hard to understand individual arrangements people might be making, but there are a range of programs and supports that the government offers to support people, particularly young people, into homeownership. There's the super saver scheme. There are also the five per cent deposits, which have been very, very popular. I saw the Minister for Housing give an update on those yesterday. But it's a bit hard to sit here and respond to a vague generalisation that you've just put forward.

Senator CHANDLER: Minister, this budget was, according to your government, about resetting intergenerational inequality. I'm trying to seek an understanding—because it is difficult to understand, based on some of the messaging about this budget—of exactly how better off young people are going to be. Will there be 35,000 fewer homes for young Australians under these tax changes, Secretary?

Ms Wilkinson : If I just come back to your previous question—and we'll see if we can give you some data on this—my understanding is that most young Australians earn most of their income through wages and salaries. The analysis that I provided in the speech that I gave last week does indeed look at what the benefits are for young Australians in all of the different circumstances that we know that they are in on the basis of the data that we have in the tax system. So if you're trying to think about how most young Australians would save up in order to place a deposit on a home, for example, most of those savings will come through wages and salaries. This is for most people. That's the only thing I would say. Sorry—what was your other question?

Senator CHANDLER: Will there be 35,000 fewer homes for young Australians under these tax changes?

Ms Wilkinson : We've outlined in detail, in box 4.4, our best estimate of what the impact of all the changes that the government announced in the budget would be on supply. We have done that modelling to the best of our abilities, and I think we've been open and transparent, in that box, about what our assessment is. What we have made clear in that box is that the direct impact of the tax changes might reduce supply by a bit, but that would be more than offset by what we estimate to be the impact on supply of the additional infrastructure measures which were also announced in the budget. So, looking at the budget overall, our assessment is that there would be an increase in net supply which would be available to first home buyers.

Senator Gallagher: There are 30,000 extra homes in the budget when you read the budget in combination with the measures and some of the changes that we're bringing forward.

Senator CHANDLER: Secretary, does that then mean that, if you didn't make the CGT changes and the negative gearing changes, there would be 35,000 more houses for young Australians to potentially purchase?

Senator HUME: Where did the $5,700 come from?

Ms Wilkinson : In the underlying spreadsheet that sat underneath that graph, there was one column which showed the impact of those three concessions—negative gearing, capital gains tax and trusts—before reform and another column which showed them after reform. The $5,700 figure was the figure after the reforms had been in place, and the $10,000—I think it's $10,200—was the figure before the reforms were in place.

Senator HUME: The speech was also criticised for erroneously stating that the OECD had claimed that capital gains tax rates are irrelevant to investment decisions. In fact, one of the authors of that OECD report said that that was highly misleading. Did you personally read the OECD paper before citing it to make that claim?

Ms Wilkinson : I reject that that was an error. That was raised with me, again, the day after the speech. I did not argue that they had no impact. The point I made—and I made it very clearly in the speech—is that OECD research suggests there is not clear evidence to support favourable treatment of capital gains to promote investment beyond compensating for inflation. I did not say that there was no case to provide concessional capital gains tax treatment. I was clear in the speech that there is a case to provide tax treatment that targets effectively innovative activity, and I highlighted in the speech a range of the measures in the budget which are designed to do exactly that.

The criticism that has been raised was not by an author of this paper. He was somebody who was listed as a contributor to the paper. I understand he worked for a short time with the team in the OECD on this paper. We have had a discussion. We discussed it before the speech, and we had a subsequent discussion after the speech with the authors of the OECD paper as to whether they considered that I misrepresented them at all in the speech, and they did not consider that I did.

Senator HUME: Can I just be very clear, though: did you read the paper?

Ms Wilkinson : Yes, I did.

Senator HUME: Let me be clear: does any other major OECD country have a capital gains tax regime like the one that's proposed for Australia?

Ms Wilkinson : One of the things that this paper does which is useful—it's one of the useful things that the OECD does—is that it can usefully provide information across a wide range of countries on all manner of things. In this particular case, it's capital gains tax treatment. There are other countries in the OECD that tax real gains. Probably the biggest country which continues to do that is Israel. Israel taxes real capital gains. That's how their system works. There are a couple of other smaller countries that do it as well. If you look at this OECD report, you can see that there is a very wide variety of ways in which capital gains taxes are treated. There are some countries that tax full nominal gains at personal income tax rates. There are some countries that tax discounted gains, like Australia and Canada do currently. There are some countries that tax all capital gains at a flat rate, so there is no tax-free threshold that applies to capital gains that are earned by individuals in that case. So there is a very wide range of different capital gains tax treatments that are applied across OECD countries. That would be the conclusion that I would draw from this analysis.

Senator HUME: On an effective capital gains tax rate, how does Australia's current regime compare to other countries? Is it substantially lower?

Ms Wilkinson : The answer to that question is that when you tax real gains, as opposed to taxing nominal gains, it varies on your circumstances. It varies on the rate of inflation in the economy, it varies on your rate of return and it varies on your tax rate and whether there is a flat-tax rate or a tax rate which is progressive, like we have in Australia's personal income tax system.

Senator HUME: Is the effective tax rate on capital gains that we have at the moment substantially lower than other countries, or is it comparable? Is it higher?

Ms Wilkinson : It depends on the returns that you're talking about, and this is traversed in budget statement No. 4 and in the document that Senator Chandler released. Unfortunately, I have to say that it depends. If one is going to accurately adjust real gains for inflation, then the effective tax rate will vary depending on the return that you have. In the document that Senator Chandler tabled, you've got to make a bunch of assumptions in order to draw any of these conclusions, and when you make those assumptions that table shows that, if you have a rate of return of around three per cent in Australia and if in the background the inflation rate is roughly three per cent, then you would face no capital gains tax. That is lower than every other country. If you have higher rates of return, then you face higher capital gains tax rates, and that varies. Whether that is higher or lower than different countries—there's quite a wide variation is the answer.

Senator HUME: My understanding is that the OECD paper suggests that Australia's current capital gains tax rate is higher, in fact, than most comparable countries, overall—our effective tax rate. In fact, Israel, which I think was the one that you cited before, has a top tax rate of only 25 per cent. Ms Wilkinson : Not in the sense that—they did not tell me how to draft this speech. Did I have a discussion with the Treasurer's office about this speech? Yes, as the Treasury secretary always does.

Senator HUME: Did they see a draft?

Ms Wilkinson : Yes.

Ms Wilkinson : Did we have a discussion about things that were in it? Yes, we had a discussion about the things I was covering in the speech. Yes.

Ms Wilkinson : I think it is completely usual, it is completely normal, for a departmental official who is providing a public speech, to have a discussion with their office about the information that is contained in the speech. The medium-term forecasting framework gives us the trend output or potential output, and that is how we get the medium-term estimates in the budget. We then receive correspondence from KPMG in relation to the specifics around the contracts they have with Treasury.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Did the letter you received yesterday relate to your contracts or to what other matters?

Ms Di Marco : They related to the services they provide and the contracts they have with the Treasury. They were not broader than that.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I know you're going to take it on notice to provide that correspondence, but what did that letter say?

Ms Di Marco : As I read out a little earlier, it covered the three items. Sorry, I don't have a hard copy with me; I will have to pick it up on my phone. It covered three main aspects. Firstly, it was to confirm that none of the matters in the notice of concern related to the performances of services to the Treasury, that they had not identified any inappropriate access or disclosure to Treasury's data and that none of the personnel engaged in connection with the services to the department were involved.

CHAIR: Senator Hume.

Senator HUME: I want to go back to the issue of productivity that Senator Canavan raised, but perhaps from a slightly different aspect. Obviously the Treasury continues to use a 1.2 per cent long-term productivity assumption. What evidence would cause Treasury to revise that assumption down?

Dr Grant : We did include a box in budget statement 2. I'm not sure if you've seen it. There are a number of factors that we have looked at when assessing the 1.2 per cent assumption for this budget. The pandemic makes it very difficult to interpret some of the recent productivity numbers. The first thing we would note is the heightened uncertainty at the moment around some of the measurement of productivity. Of course, all that's happening geopolitically in terms of trade tensions is not positive for productivity but, as we've seen, the global economy has been more resilient than we thought on the back of a lot of technology investment. We are seeing some of that data centre investment in Australia. In this box we talk about some of the upside and downside. We believe there's both upside and downside to that number. We also look at what other international agencies are doing with their long-term assumption, partly because they're well informed agencies and good to speak to about these things. It's also partly because the global frontier matters for Australia. Having a sense of where others think that will be is important. We did try to say there's a lot of uncertainty always around productivity and outlined our assessment for this budget. In that box we did make a change to the transition period to the long-term assumption. We thought it was better to be a little more in line with what others were doing. It does take a little time for productivity to lift. We put that at around five years.

Senator HUME: What is the current probability weighted risk that that assumption is too high?

Dr Grant : I don't have the probability of that.

Senator HUME: I'll phrase it a different way, because I know you've done this work previously. Could you outline potentially what the budget impacts would be if productivity growth was not 1.2 per cent and instead was only 0.7 per cent, 0.9 per cent or one per cent over the medium term?

Dr Grant : We did include some sensitivity analysis in the Intergenerational report 2023, which does in fact do this. Around the 1.2 per cent—it then looked at productivity growth of 0.9 per cent versus 1.5 per cent. So 1.2 per cent is in the middle. As you can imagine, it does matter quite a bit. Productivity matters in the long run, even small changes. We report in the IGR—and I'll just make sure Mr McDonald doesn't want to jump in; I hope I don't misread the numbers—that, if productivity growth were 0.3 percentage points higher, the level of real and nominal GDP would have been around 9.5 per cent higher in 2062-63—so in the long run. Of course, that would have meant the underlying cash deficit as a share of GDP would have been smaller because of higher real and nominal GDP growth.

Senator HUME: Have you then calculated 0.3 per cent productivity growth? That was the current figure in the national accounts from March last year to March this year.

Dr Grant : Productivity in the national accounts at the quarterly level is incredibly volatile. We haven't done any calculations beyond those published in the 2023 IGR when it comes to the sensitivity analysis, but the volatility means we will try to look at longer term trends than the latest quarterly results.

Senator HUME: Let me ask you in a different way: how does Treasury reconcile its 1.2 per cent long-term assumption with the Reserve Bank's downgrade of trend productivity back down to 0.7 per cent over its forecast horizon?

Dr Grant : Over the same period—so in the detailed forecast period, the near term—we are about the same in our assumptions. We are lifting the trend of productivity growth or the underlying measure slowly over about five years. In the near-term forecasts, it is very close to the RBA numbers and then lifts over time.

Senator HUME: How long is the RBA's forecast horizon compared to Treasury's?

Dr Grant : They only do the detailed forecast period of two to three years whereas we forecast the four to five over the forward estimates.

Senator HUME: If you have some insights that the RBA doesn't, can you outline for me the government policies that are expected to make the largest quantifiable contribution to productivity growth and over what timeframe they kick in?

Dr Grant : Can I make sure I understand your question? Could you ask me again?

Senator HUME: Could you provide a list, for instance, of the top 10 policies that are in the budget that Treasury has calculated as having a net positive impact on productivity? Can you give me a sense of the percentage increase that each policy is calculated in providing?

Dr Grant : We don't look at policy from a bottom-up perspective in the medium term, but in terms of the policies that the government has in this budget where they are focused on productivity there is a range of measures to reduce red tape. Reducing compliance burden should help productivity in Australia. Removing barriers to trade is also something we would imagine would be positive for productivity in the long term. In terms of the single national market, making it easier to work across the borders of the states and territories is also important for helping business to operate smoothly in Australia. Accelerating approvals is another one that is coming to my mind. They are the ones that come to my mind as making a difference, but we didn't quantify—

Senator HUME: You don't do a bottom-up? If we fast-track approvals, rewrite the EPBC or whatever it might be, you don't say, 'That will add X per cent to productivity growth'?

Dr Grant : Our Markets Group would have a sense of the regulatory burden that is being lifted, so that would be an indication. But you are right. We don't get down to bit by bit or policy by policy.

Senator HUME: Let me tackle this in a slightly different way. In 2022, the former Treasury secretary told this committee that 'if we had zero productivity growth, wage growth consistent with stable inflation of 2½ per cent would be 2½ per cent' and that 'if we had productivity growth of one per cent a year, wage growth consistent with inflation of 2½ per cent would be 3½ per cent, and, if we had 1½ per cent productivity growth, it would be four per cent'. Is that a view that's still held by the department?

Dr Grant : That is the long-run relationship. That is an important caveat, but, yes, you will see in the forward estimates of our economic parameters that over the medium term wages growth finds its steady state at exactly the relationship that you have just pointed out.

Senator HUME: Terrific. Given those recent figures that show that productivity growth is at 0.3 per cent through the past 12 months and inflation is at 4.2 per cent, what would an inflationary wage increase figure be?

Dr Grant : That is difficult for me to make a broad comment on simply because in the near term the labour supply and labour demand dynamics do matter. In the aggregate that we have in the economic parameters—let me check that I have the right number in my head—we have wage growth growing at 3¼ per cent to the June quarter of 2026 and 3½ per cent to the June quarter of 2027. That is our assessment of wage growth that is in line with the economic fundamentals in that year.

Senator HUME: The first one was 3.25 per cent wage growth—

Dr Grant : Through the year to the June quarter of 2026, yes.

Senator HUME: If you then add—and I know that we're about one-quarter off here—3.25 per cent wage growth to 0.3 per cent productivity, does that lead to inflation heading back to the 2.25 per cent band? Does that lead to a stable inflation rate?

Dr Grant : The issue is that the relationship holds in the long run. In the near term there can be a whole lot of things that can influence where you think an economy settles. In the long run that relationship, which is the inflation and the productivity numbers, gives you wage growth. The balance isn't found in the short term with that relationship; that is a long-term relationship.

Senator HUME: In the short term, you don't think that the current productivity growth level is consistent with a stable return to low inflation. Do you in the medium term—

Dr Grant : I didn't say that. All I'm trying to say is that when we do the economic forecast in the very immediate term—each sector, each market—we are trying to look at exactly what is happening within it. You can have a number of factors influencing the economy. Where you think the economy settles at reflects that long-term relationship, but that relationship doesn't have to hold steady through any economic cycle.

Senator HUME: I want to ask some questions about how Treasury measures employment growth to assist in the calculation of productivity projections, or is that something that Treasury leaves to the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations?

Dr Grant : We do the employment growth forecast in the budget.

Senator HUME: Do you split that measurement between the market and non-market sector?

Dr Grant : Not in the forecast, no. We do aggregate employment.

Senator HUME: Do you use the same definitions as the ABS in your forecast?

Dr Grant : Yes.

Senator HUME: The ABS does determine which jobs fall within each sector?

Dr Grant : They report that, yes.

Senator HUME: You could do that, but you just don't; is that right?

Dr Grant : If you think about employment in the economy and what drives it, it's activity. We don't have activity forecasts on the market and the non-market sector. We look at the aggregate. In line with that, we look at aggregate employment.

Senator HUME: Does Treasury then measure productivity improvements in non-market services where the output quality is not necessarily priced through markets? Is that something that Treasury would look at?

Dr Grant : We look at it in history, absolutely, but again in terms of the long-term assumption that is an aggregate assumption.

Senator HUME: Has Treasury assessed whether public sector employment growth is crowding out labour from higher productivity market sectors?

Dr Grant : I might ask Mr McDonald to comment in terms of some of the more recent forecast assessments. Again, at an aggregate level, I don't think we are seeing that in the economy. You are correct that the non-market employment did grow strongly for a period. That's now crossed back over, and we have market employment picking up. We do pay attention to what we think is driving the aggregate numbers underneath, and you'll always see different sectors grow at different rates.

Mr H McDonald: Previously there has been strong non-market sector employment growth, but, in the December quarter 2025, the market sector contributed 65.5 per cent of employment growth through the year. That's reflecting both a moderation of the growth in non-market and the underlying strength in the market employment.

Senator HUME: Was that for the quarter or for the year?

Mr H McDonald: It's through the year to the December quarter.

Senator HUME: There are some senior economists, and I have a report in my hand from one of them, who have looked at—

Senator Gallagher: From where?

Senator HUME: Sorry, this is from Westpac. They have looked at the employment shift that's occurred in the economy from the market to the non-market sector. In this document, one of the economists said that this has been 'unprecedented and represents a substantially larger labour market reallocation that occurred during the mining investment boom, owing to the far greater labour intensity of public services relative to mining'. The document also said that '40 per cent of total employment is now linked to public spending', which is almost nine points higher than a decade ago. Is Treasury doing any analysis on what the impact of that shift might have on productivity?

Dr Grant : I can ask Mr Lawson. His division will often do analysis on productivity. What I think we're referring to here is the growth that we are seeing in some of the healthcare sectors. We saw that show up in the numbers. You are exactly right in that the measurement of productivity in some of those sectors is difficult. Mr Lawson, did you have anything—

Senator Gallagher: It's the care economy—the big shift. We need to make sure there are jobs in aged care, early education care and disability care. It is part of the reason we have some reforms for the NDIS as well.

Mr Lawson : I have a few observations. One is that this trend towards an increase in the relative growth of the non-market sector has been common across the advanced economies. This is not an Australia-specific phenomenon. I think that's quite important context. That expansion of the non-market sector does reflect changing consumption preferences in the economy. Demographic shifts such as Australia's ageing population are very important. That growth is being driven in significant part by demand for health- and aged-care services. The healthcare and social assistance industry, which is a very important part, has increased from eight per cent of the workforce to 16 per cent in early 2026, so that's over a 32-year period. Some of this is also related to the formalisation and marketisation of services that were previously paid for and not measured in economic statistics. You also have to take into account the way that it can be very difficult to measure productivity in the non-market sector. There's a range of issues that are taking place here influencing the relative growth rate of the market and the non-market sector and then how that's reflected in formally measured productivity and the measurement area around that.

Senator HUME: What issues are you tracking that you see as influential on your forecasts of not only productivity but also participation? Do you do work on labour market mobility et cetera?

Dr Grant : Yes, we do. In the economic forecast, we have the labour force participation rate rising a little further. We believe women are supporting that quite a bit. Also, older cohorts are participating more. We look at the participation rate. We also look at average hours, not only in the near term but also over the medium term, and then productivity. The recent labour account also gives us a sense of the labour market, how many people are holding multiple jobs and what kind of job switching is happening across the economy. It is continuing to show that, while there has been a little softening in the labour market, it's still by historical standards holding up relatively well.

Senator HUME: I assume you track external changes such as the fuel crisis and the effect that would have on productivity as well; does that feed in?

Dr Grant : We assess it. It is very hard; when we say that the extent and the duration of this shock is going to matter, that matters in the near term for the forecast. It will also matter for the world and then whether the world makes any more significant adjustments or finds it difficult to cope if this shock continues on. We assess it, but, again, it is very difficult—particularly in a shock that is occurring at the moment.

Senator HUME: What about changes to state legislation or domestic policy settings that might be outside Treasury's control? How do you factor that in?

Dr Grant : We do speak to state and territory counterparts. In a sense, in ongoing conversations with states and territories, some of them do have their own productivity assumptions; some of those are lower than the 1.2. We have conversations with them around what they think are factors driving their own assessments. We try to understand their view and their perspective on it as well.

Senator HUME: Do you track how Commonwealth measures are impacting productivity or your projections?

Dr Grant : In the sense of within—

Senator HUME: What about the government's energy policy? What about the government's industrial relations changes? Do those things factor into your projections?

Dr Grant : Again, at a broad level of assessment rather than from a bottom-up perspective—but, yes, we have got to have a sense of what we think will impact productivity across the whole economy.

Senator HUME: Isn't there a productivity policy that's Treasury's responsibility; is that right? Are you still responsible for productivity policy?

Dr Grant : Markets Group are doing a lot in this space. In addition, I think Markets Group would tell you other departments are also doing a lot in this space, but Markets Group would be able to speak to the specific policy details.

Senator Gallagher: The ones that Treasury has responsibility for.

Senator HUME: There's a whole-of-government regulatory reform agenda, and the fact sheet was produced. Is Markets Group the correct place in which to ask that question?

Senator Gallagher: We dealt with that in Finance.

Senator HUME: Did Treasury have input into the creation of that fact sheet?

Senator Gallagher: Yes, in the sense that the Treasurer and I work across it together, but policy responsibility sits with me as Minister for Finance.

Senator HUME: I might have some follow-up questions on that.

CHAIR: Senator McDonald.

Senator McDONALD: I have some questions in terms of the Commonwealth's taxation revenue from the PRRT. It's been reported that Treasury has been requested to do modelling for another potential change.

Senator Gallagher: That would be more appropriately asked of Revenue Group.

Senator McDONALD: I'll see you later in the day on that. For the mining investment forecast predictions in Budget Paper No. 1, at page 62, the forecast for the domestic economy shows that investment into the mining industry is expected to drop to zero growth in 2027-28. Is Treasury aware of why that could be causing this figure and what impact that can have economically?

Dr Grant : I will ask Mr McDonald to come in on this question. This is just the growth rate. While the growth rates are low, the level of mining investment is quite high at the moment. This is a sector that goes through bursts of investment and will then pull back a little bit, but not the level. The level holds. I think they've undertaken quite a bit of investment recently, so the growth in investment slows in the near term. Let me just check that I'm correct.

Mr H McDonald: That's correct. The growth in investment does slow in the forecast, but the level is at a historically elevated level in terms of the capital stock in the mining sector. Obviously we talked about pipelines in housing before, but pipelines in mining investment matter as well. What we're seeing in terms of exploration pipelines is that mineral exploration expenditure rose by 6.3 per cent in the March quarter, driven by iron ore, whereas petroleum exploration expenditure fell by 4.8 per cent in that same quarter.

Senator McDONALD: Why is it that last Thursday the IEA released the latest World energy investment report, which made specific findings with regard to Australia—particularly in the critical mineral space—and, in terms of investment, singled out Australia by name? It said:

Exploration spending for critical minerals also weakened, with activity falling in Australia (-30%) …

Dr Grant : I haven't read the detail of that report.

Senator McDONALD: At the same time, exploration spending in Asia, particularly South Asia, increased by 20 per cent.

Dr Grant : In terms of the sectoral breakdown, I don't have any of that in front of me. We could take that on notice. I refer to the national accounts that came out earlier this week. I had a recollection that it was quite strong through the year. Recently, the national accounts showed a small fall in mineral and petroleum exploration in the March quarter, but it is small because it's growing at 19.1 per cent through the year.

Senator McDONALD: Isn't it extraordinary that the world is looking at Australia's data and saying that we've fallen by 30 per cent? This is a point I was making to the resources department yesterday and to DISR. We have to be very careful to understand that we live in a competitive world. If Australian investment is falling off a cliff in our mining sector—the part of the economy that pays the bills—we should be very concerned about that. I'm surprised that Treasury has not been alerted to the IEA's report?

Dr Grant : We tend to rely on the national accounts. We can have a look at that data source. This does show relatively strong mineral and petroleum exploration. One thing that can happen is, if this is happening in a particular part of the mining industry, it might not show up in the aggregate numbers. If one part of the mining industry were investing $100 and then they stopped doing that and another did, you wouldn't see that in the aggregates; you would see that in sectoral shifts. It might be a sectoral shift. We can have a look.

Senator McDONALD: That is an interesting point you make, because so much of Treasury modelling is around growth in critical minerals. It is a sector that has smaller tonnages, smaller prices and smaller commodities, yet somehow that is magically going to replace iron ore, coal, gas and, I guess, now gold as our big income earners. It perplexes me that Treasury is modelling that the growth in critical minerals is going to replace those core commodity groups.

Dr Grant : I think you might be referring to the Net Zero Plan modelling and the renewable upside scenario. I make the point that our climate modelling scenario base is very different from core forecasts over the forward estimates. They are different.

Senator McDONALD: You're right; I did have some questions about that. Under that modelling, you see fossil fuel exports collapsing despite having worldwide records in demand for coal and gas each consecutive year. The modelling is that it will collapse, and instead we will have green commodities replacing those—it's a bit of a hard graph to read—by about 2032.

Dr Grant : You are correct. In the sense that report published a baseline scenario, then published a renewable exports upside scenario and then a disorderly transition scenario, all of those are based on a range of assumptions including global climate change policies. I would make the point: please treat that as scenario modelling done, which was the renewable upside scenario.

Senator McDONALD: It also models fossil fuel exports collapsing when we know that each year we have seen record demand for coal and gas in particular. Oil has also leapt to the forefront of our minds. However, that baseline just seems to be completely at odds with what's happening in worldwide markets.

Dr Grant : Again, the scenario baseline is not the budget forecast. I make the point that this was done to inform the Net Zero Plan. When it comes to the forward estimates and the budget parameters, we largely hold the terms of trade flat by the end of the detailed forecast period. I want to be clear that this isn't driving any of the aggregate economic parameters in the budget statement.

Senator McDONALD: Why would Treasury produce modelling that is so far removed from the reality of the data that Treasury is using to forecast the budget?

Dr Grant : We wouldn't characterise it that way. We would say that this is scenario modelling where we were trying to show what could happen on the upside and the downside to a baseline Net Zero Plan modelling case. This is very long-term modelling. The intergenerational report is where we do the long-term modelling, whereas when we do the budget parameters we are dealing with much shorter timeframes.

Senator McDONALD: Regardless, this modelling is fanciful. It's ideological. If there is one person in Treasury using a minute of time to model something that shows that two of Australia's biggest exports are in massive decline, which they are not, I think you're wasting your time and, worse, setting up budget parameters and expenditure that is not in Australia's best interests and doesn't reflect reality. I'm really surprised that Treasury would have any part of its division doing that work.

Dr Grant : In terms of this modelling, it was done to support the government's policy around the Net Zero Plan. We were very open and transparent about the assumptions and released a fairly detailed appendix with all of those assumptions. It is often the case that scenario modelling is done to show what could happen under different circumstances. Often, our job is to show that or the risks. That was the intent with which we undertook this modelling.

Senator McDONALD: Normally, though, you'd use reality as a portion of the modelling, wouldn't you? This has no basis in reality. It's not supported by your budget forecasts, the International Energy Agency forecasts or exports as they stand right now. There's no intersection between that part of reality and what has been modelled here.

Dr Grant : Again, we based it on a renewable exports upside scenario. That is a possibility. Everyone will have a different perspective on the possibilities when it comes to long-term scenario modelling. I can promise you that a lot of care and effort goes into trying to show all of the assumptions, how we did it and then what the results are. That's all we were trying to do.

Senator McDONALD: Which part of the team would do this work? Is that the Macroeconomic Group?

Dr Grant : Yes. We have a branch that focuses on climate and industry modelling—long-term structural modelling.

Senator McDONALD: They must be a lot of fun; they live in a different universe!

CHAIR: Senator Hume.

Senator HUME: I refer back to this fact sheet on regulatory reform. In the appendix, there's a breakdown of the regulatory burden reduction. This is the $10.2 billion a year in gross regulatory burden reduction. I know that the minister has said that this was the responsibility of Finance, not Treasury, but did Treasury have any input into it?

Dr Grant : Yes, Markets Group in particular. We were consulted on some of it. I understand there may be a GDP number in that fact sheet. Markets Group were the main lead on that from Treasury and, like usual, Macro Group often consulted throughout that process.

Senator HUME: Does Macro Group cast its eye over the validity of some of the costings of the estimates?

Dr Grant : Not so much the costing. In terms of the regulatory burden, we did not. In relation to the GDP figure, Markets Group calculates a long-run figure. We did take a look at that.

Senator Gallagher: There was work done across government. You can see the different measures. Environment would have been involved with the EPBC one. The big ones are in housing and environment, but there was whole-of-government work done on trying to land the gross regulatory reduction.

Senator HUME: This measure outlines a number of decisions on programs that will 'increase productivity'. Was the department consulted on how these measures would increase productivity?

Senator Gallagher: It forms one element of the productivity package in the budget but, if you look at streamlining environment-EPBC assessment pathways, clearly that's going to have an impact.

Senator HUME: That's what I want to know.

Senator Gallagher: That's one of the big areas that business has been asking for.

Senator HUME: Is there a quantum on the productivity uplift on each of those measures? I know that you have a dollar figure about—

Senator Gallagher: Yes, that's the way we're trying to measure it.

Senator HUME: You're reducing the regulatory burden. You put a dollar figure on the reduction of regulatory burden but not necessarily on a productivity quantum?

Senator Gallagher: All of these measures work towards supporting the productivity forecast in the budget, as previous evidence has heard. It forms one element—reducing red tape or regulatory reduction—but all of removing barriers to trade, building a single national market, accelerating approvals, simplifying building regulations, building more homes and modernising the energy system contributes to supporting the forecasts that Treasury has outlined in the budget.

Senator HUME: Some of those on the list have caveats, the first being that some of the measures are subject to agreement by state and territory governments. Does Treasury have a time line on what year we can expect the full $10.2 billion of productivity uplift being realised?

Dr Grant : The $10.2 billion is the regulatory—

Senator HUME: Sorry, I should have said that it was the regulatory burden being realised as opposed to productivity being realised.

Dr Grant : Markets Group will be able to answer your questions on that.

Senator Gallagher: Noting that it is a matter for which the Department of Finance is responsible and that we did go through this last week.

Senator HUME: It's a gross figure?

Senator Gallagher: Yes.

Senator HUME: Why is that?

Senator Gallagher: Because we're trying to measure these elements of the budget measures.

Senator HUME: Why not measure all elements of the budget as to what the regulatory burden may be?

Senator Gallagher: In relation to the regulatory reforms that we are bringing in in this budget, this is the way that we have chosen to measure it.

Senator HUME: But you're only measuring the regulatory burdens that you feel that you're removing, not the regulatory burdens that you're imposing.

Senator Gallagher: We're being very clear that this is a gross regulatory burden reduction. I think we're being very upfront about that.

Senator HUME: Are you being upfront about what the net imposition or removal of regulatory burden is?

Senator Gallagher: The budget figure has a gross reduction.

Senator HUME: That's like reporting revenue and not payments. Why not use a net figure?

Senator Gallagher: This is the first time that I can recall us putting a measurement essentially around reducing regulatory burden. We will continue to look at ways to measure it. Hopefully, you might vote for some of it; you voted against the first bill we brought to the parliament.

Senator HUME: When do you think the $10.2 billion per year in gross regulatory burden will be realised?

Senator Gallagher: As we said, we are pressing on with it. Some of it requires you to support the regulatory reform bill that is being introduced with the budget.

Senator HUME: National competition policy?

Senator Gallagher: If you say no in the Senate and we can't get that bill through, that will have an impact. That is the approach you took on the first regulatory reduction burden. Last year, you voted against the regulatory reduction omnibus bill.

Senator HUME: I'm simply asking when you think the number that you've put in the budget, as selective as it is, is going to be realised?

Senator Gallagher: It's not selective. In consultation with pre-budget key priorities, business wanted an effort put in on regulatory reduction. We have done that. Hopefully, you will support some of it, noting that you don't support housing elements and, from memory, you didn't support the EPBC. You were already opposed to the big components, but we will press on and try to ensure all of these elements are delivered.

Senator HUME: Half of it's dependent on negotiation with the states, isn't it?

Senator Gallagher: Unlike your government, we work with states and territories. In terms of building more housing and on planning reforms, the Commonwealth does not have those powers. Yes, we work with the states and territories on that. Are you suggesting we shouldn't and therefore just leave planning reform to somebody else to care about?

Senator HUME: The understanding is it's $10.2 billion, but only if everything goes your way, and it's over a time period that no-one can determine.

Senator Gallagher: Senator Hume, with your support we will be able to deliver that very quickly.

Senator HUME: No, you need the states.

Senator Gallagher: On all of the other elements that we need, like including the tell-us-once reforms, help us with those. In terms of simplifying the tax system, put your votes where your concerns are and support regulatory reform. I haven't seen any evidence of your doing that.

Senator HUME: Is it the Commonwealth or the states that are doing the heavy lifting here?

Senator Gallagher: It's the Commonwealth in partnership with the states, particularly on housing, to some degree with the competition policy and where there are shared responsibilities under EPBC. But that is the federation. That's the way it is.

Senator HUME: The package is pretty much a rough figure, reliant on others to do the work and we don't know when it will be delivered?

Senator Gallagher: Senator Hume, you have a role to play here. You could support this.

CHAIR: We're going to have to rotate the call.

Senator Gallagher: We haven't seen any indication that you will. Talk it down. That's fine. We expect that from you.

Senator HUME: I'm just trying to understand it.

Senator Gallagher: We are being clear that it's about a gross reduction. We've outlined the measures that we think deliver that outcome and we are absolutely determined to deliver them.

Senator HUME: Lastly, there is a regulatory burden imposed by the tax changes, and that's been made clear. Why wouldn't you at least include that, because you know what that is? Why would you not include that in a breakdown of regulatory burden?

Senator Gallagher: We've reported against the gross regulatory reduction.

Senator HUME: So only the good stuff and not the bad stuff?

Senator Gallagher: I'll leave you to editorialise as you choose. What's more important is voting for and helping deliver these changes, particularly the ones that come to the Senate.

Senator HUME: We're going to vote against the tax cuts and that way we're going to improve the regulatory burden on Australians.

Senator Gallagher: You're voting against the tax cuts right now. I don't know if you noticed, but those bells going right now is you voting against tax cuts.

Senator HUME: No, we're voting against your increased taxes, and that will reduce the regulatory burden on Australians.

Senator Gallagher: The bells have been going all morning and you are ultimately going to vote against tax cuts today—right now—that make a difference for people.

Senator HUME: Net tax increases are what we're voting against today.

Senator Gallagher: No, let's be clear what you're voting against. Yes, you're voting against tax reform but you're also voting against the instant tax deduction, the $1,000, and the weighting. That's what you're doing today.

Senator HUME: Is the legislation that's in the House of Representatives today a net tax increase or decrease?
