We work to support a reliable, efficient and competitive payment system; we deliver efficient, effective banking services to Australian government agencies; and we provide secure and reliable bank notes. Since the February estimates hearings, the Monetary Policy Board has increased the cash rate to help return inflation to target. I'm going to briefly outline recent developments in the Australian and global economy. I'm going to discuss inflation and the outlook and then I'm going to conclude with some remarks on the bank's work on payments, including the recent review of card payments and what we call Project Acacia.

In the first half of 2025, you may recall that inflation was coming down and had declined to be within our target range of two to three per cent. Labour market conditions were easing and employment growth was slowing and, of course, there was significant uncertainty, if you recall, about the economic outlook driven by developments in global trade policy. At the time the board judged that capacity pressures would continue to ease and that it was appropriate to remove some restrictiveness from the stance of monetary policy by lowering interest rates.

Inflation picked up notably in the second half of 2025 and, to date, it remains too high. This increase in inflation reflected a strong increase in output growth, which has added to existing capacity pressures in the economy and tightness in the labour market. Inflation was too high even before the conflict in the Middle East began. The conflict has led to a sharp increase in oil and other key commodity prices. This has already pushed inflation higher through higher consumer fuel prices. We've also seen some tentative signs that higher fuel related costs may have been passed through into the cost of other goods and services, including new dwelling costs, and there are indications that there are likely to be second-round effects on the prices of goods and services more broadly. As I mentioned, this inflation impulse is in addition to the high inflation recorded in the start of 2026.

Developments in the Middle East remain highly uncertain but, under a wide range of scenarios, the conflict could well contribute to even higher global and domestic inflation. The effects of the conflict on economic activity are less certain and expected to vary across countries, but for Australia we judge that it will weigh modestly on growth. This would worsen the trade-off between inflation and economic activity.

As you know, the Monetary Policy Board has increased the cash rate by 75 basis points in total this year. These increases have been necessary to tighten financial conditions and slow growth and demand in the economy to ensure we get on top of inflation. We've already seen some signs that this tightening is starting to work, though it will take around one to two years for the full effects to fully flow through to the economy.

One of the channels through which monetary policy can often start to have an impact quite quickly is the housing market. Conditions in the housing market have been eased in recent months and that partly reflects tighter monetary policy. Having said that, the recent increases in interest rates will have no impact on the increase in inflation already in train following the increases in the prices of oil and related commodities. What these increases in the cash rate do, however, is help to contain the domestic inflationary pressures and second-round effects from higher oil and commodity prices.

I recognise that this is a difficult time for many households facing cost-of-living pressures, but it is important we bring inflation under control. If high inflation persists, it risks becoming embedded in price and wage-setting behaviour, particularly given the prolonged period over which underlying inflation has been above three per cent since the pandemic. This would result in more persistent inflation and would require even higher interest rates, and for longer, to return inflation to target. High inflation hurts everyone, it reduces the purchasing power of all Australians, and it disproportionately affects those on lower incomes and the more vulnerable people in the community.

You may know we published our latest forecast in the May Statement on monetary policy. Overall, the flow of data and developments since May has not been materially different to our expectations, but we will publish a full update to these forecasts in August. We expect inflation to increase further in the near term. In our baseline forecast published in May, headline inflation is expected to peak at over 4.5 per cent in the June quarter, while underlying inflation remains above the target range until the middle of 2027.

GDP growth is expected to slow this year, reflecting the effects of higher interest rates and the conflict in the Middle East. We expect the unemployment rate to increase over the coming year or so but still remain lower than before the pandemic. We will be carefully monitoring conditions to assess how the combined effects of higher interest rates and the energy price shock are playing out.

Employment is expected to continue growing gradually over time. It's worth noting that the share of population with a job remains high, notwithstanding recent declines. This is a welcome development for those individuals and their families and the wider Australian economy. Our forecasts are just that, and the outlook is highly uncertain. Alongside our most recent set of forecasts we published two adverse scenarios that outline how the economy could evolve under a larger or more prolonged conflict in the Middle East. This would increase commodity prices further and would result in higher inflation and weaker growth than currently forecast. While these are challenging conditions, the economy is still expected to grow, although modestly, even under these scenarios where oil prices are significantly higher than recent levels.

Investment has been a bright spot recently and growth is expected to continue in sectors of the economy with strong structural tailwinds such as software, data centres and renewable energy. The Monetary Policy Board will continue to assess the incoming data and developments here and abroad. Having raised the cash rate three times, monetary policy is well placed to respond to developments. Inflation is too high and the board will do what it considers necessary to achieve our mandate to deliver high stability and full employment.

Finally, I will briefly highlight some of the bank's work on payments. Following our review of card payments, we announced three key changes: surcharging on debit and credit cards should end from 1 October, we're lowering interchange fee caps on debit and consumer credit cards, and we're improving transparency on payment costs. Together, these reforms will simplify payments for consumers and improve outcomes for businesses.

In addition, the bank, in partnership with the Digital Finance Cooperative Research Centre, recently published the findings of Project Acacia. This work explored how tokenisation of assets and money would enhance the functioning of Australia's wholesale markets. The project found that there is growing industry interest in the potential for tokenisation to improve efficiency and reduce risk in wholesale financial markets. Similar momentum is building in key financial centres around the world.

The bank is now in the planning phase on a range of subsequent initiatives aimed at promoting responsible financial innovation and ensuring the Australian financial system is well positioned for the digital age. Thank you. My colleagues and I are happy to take your questions.

CHAIR: Thank you very much, Ms Bullock. We will go first to Senator Chandler.

Senator CHANDLER: Thank you, Governor and officials, for your time this afternoon. Has the Reserve Bank formed a view on whether the overall fiscal impulse from this budget is adding to or subtracting from aggregate demand?

Ms Bullock : I think, in our assessment at the moment—and we would wait to see what is legislated—if everything goes according to plan, we don't see that it's much different than what we were foreseeing in MYEFO.

Senator CHANDLER: The budget includes significant new household transfers, including the fuel excise cut, the $1,000 instant tax deduction and cost-of-living measures. Has the RBA assessed whether these measures are likely to be stimulatory to demand at a time when inflation isn't yet sustainably back in target range?

Ms Bullock : What matters for inflation is demand relative to supply, and fiscal public demand adds to aggregate demand. Our assessment is that for public demand relative to our forecast in May this budget is not adding anything further to public demand than it was adding in our forecast.

Dr Hunter : We don't just consider the federal budget, of course. We realise that's your focus, given this is federal parliament, but we have to look at the whole picture. The states are very important in all of this; they account for the majority of government investment, for example, and about half of current consumption. We're also waiting until we get the full set of state forecasts—certainly the big state forecasts—because they matter in all of this as well.

Senator CHANDLER: To be clear, the RBA hasn't done any specific assessments on those household transfers that I talked about?

Ms Bullock : The household transfer is a part of public demand and what we look at is the aggregate. We don't do individual assessments of individual components of the budget. We focus on what the bottom line of public demand is in the budget. To the extent that there is something there and there are give-and-takes in other areas, what matters is the total.

Senator CHANDLER: You've said that there's nothing additional being provided from the policies that are in this budget. It's fair to say, isn't it, that a high level of public demand is already built into your forecast? Is that correct?

Ms Bullock : We've got a level of demand and you can make a judgement on what's high and low. I'm not making a judgement on that. I'm just saying there is a certain amount of public demand baked into our forecasts. When eventually things get legislated, then we will incorporate them into our forecast. At the moment, based on what we've seen, we're not seeing additional public demand. It looks very similar to what we were seeing at MYEFO. I caution what Dr Hunter said though, of course, because there are still state budgets to come.

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry, just so we're very clear, in terms of when something is legislated, does that mean that your forecast will change when the parliament passes the package that we've started the process of today?

Ms Bullock : No, I'm not saying that. I'm saying, if everything goes as the government has put out in its budget, then in terms of the public demand profile it does not look very different to what it looked like last time we did our forecast. It's not adding or subtracting; it's just what it is.

Senator CHANDLER: Public demand is growing at 3.7 per cent this year in your forecast; is that correct?

Dr Hunter : Yes, that's our forecast from May that we put out just before the federal budget. We expect through to the June quarter this year that the year-on-year increase in public demand would be 3.7 per cent and then you can see that growth rate tailing off as you move through the next two years of the forecast horizon that we have.

Senator CHANDLER: That is 2.8 per cent next year; that's correct?

Dr Hunter : Yes, through to June 2027; that's right.

Senator CHANDLER: That's still much faster than real GDP growth, though, isn't it?

Dr Hunter : It is faster than we expect real GDP growth to be at that point; obviously, it's a forecast. Just to clarify, when the Governor was saying about what's legislated, what we care about is what's actually going to happen. We wait to see what actually is implemented. It's not a question of what's in papers or what's in the newspapers or anything. It's what is actually implemented. The next point for us is August, which will be more than enough time for us to have a look at for what is actually implemented between now and then.

Senator CHANDLER: On the Working Australians Tax Offset, which will commence in 2027-28, has the RBA had any engagement with Treasury about the timing of that measure from a monetary policy perspective?

Ms Bullock : No.

Senator CHANDLER: Governor, can you confirm the RBA's current central expectation of when the cash rate will return to a more neutral setting and whether that expectation has been revised since the budget was handed down.

Ms Bullock: I probably should just be very clear here, Senator. When you see assumptions about the cash rate in our forecast, they are assumptions. They are not our expectations. They are market expectations, and we use them as a conditioning assumption on which to base our forecasts. So they are not our expectations. Now, having said that, they are market expectations, and market expectations at the moment are for one more increase in the cash rate—I'm going to defer to Chris here—by the end of the year and then a slight decline, I think, next year. But, Chris, did you want to re elaborate?

Dr Kent : No—just to reinforce exactly what you just mentioned, Michele. But, with regard to the budget, what we do when we bed down our forecasts is look at what the market expectation is and then use that for our forecast. That's an assumption; that's very mechanical. That market expectation has eased a bit since we did the forecasts, in May, but that was not following the budget. That was following some slightly weaker data than markets had expected on the monthly inflation and then the monthly labour force data.

Senator CHANDLER: The government has made a number of statements about the relationship between government spending and the task that you have as the RBA. Does the board share the government's characterisation that its budget settings, including Commonwealth spending being at a 40-year high as a share of the economy in 2026-27, will support the return of inflation to target range?

Ms Bullock: The board doesn't have a view on the government's budget. The board basically is focusing on what the difference between aggregate demand and aggregate supply is as inflation. It takes the rest as given and is going to adjust monetary policy appropriately.

Senator CHANDLER: Just back to some questions that I did go over with Treasury earlier on today—so, if you were listening along, apologies if they're a bit repetitive. It's been widely reported that there are significant differences between Treasury's near-term forecasts and your near-term forecasts. In 2026-27, the RBA is forecasting 1.4 per cent, while Treasury is forecasting 1.75. And, in the next financial year, again, the RBA forecasts 1.4 and Treasury is forecasting 2.25. So there is a real difference there, and it is growing. Can you please outline the reasons for this difference?

Ms Bullock: I'll make a couple of opening remarks and then I'm going to pass to Sarah for some details. The first point I would make is that forecasts are forecasts, and reasonable people can differ on forecasts. The second point I would make is that we talk to Treasury, but we do have differences of opinions on some things, and one of the things, I think, is on the gap between access demand—aggregate demand and aggregate supply. But I'm going to pass to Sarah because I think she has more of the detail on this.

Dr Hunter: I reiterate Michele's first point. I think that's really almost the most crucial point here—that economists and reasonable people more broadly will definitely hold different views as to the outlook and how things are going to play out. In terms of the GDP forecasts specifically, I thought I'd talk a bit to what's underpinning ours and why we land where we do and what I understand are some of the differences with Treasury. But, before I do that, I also wanted to just point out that other aspects of the forecasts are actually pretty similar across the two institutions. In particular, the outlook for the labour market is pretty similar, and the outlook for inflation as well. So, on this one aspect, there is a bit of a gap, but it's not uniformly replicated across all of those key economic indicators.

In terms of our forecast, we think that the economy is going to go into a bit of a slowdown now. In fact, we saw a slowing in growth momentum on the quarter in the national accounts data that we got yesterday. That wasn't a surprise. In fact, the data yesterday was broadly in line with what we were expecting, but we can come back to that. And so, by the time we get through to the June quarter next year, we think that GDP growth momentum, as you said, will be around 1.4 per cent, so 1½ per cent or near enough. That's slightly below the pace that we think the economy can sustain on a trend basis, which is around two per cent. You could also describe that as the pace at which the economy's supply capacity is growing. And we think it will stay at around that pace of growth, as you noted, through to 2028.

That's really a product of the fact that we think the cash rate settings that we assumed in our forecast horizon—to reiterate what the governor said earlier about them being an assumption, not an expectation or an internal judgement. We think that the cash rate holding at around 4.6 or 4.7 per cent, which is the technical assumption—you can see it in the SMP—will mean that it's somewhat restrictive. That being restrictive means that growth momentum in the economy—so the pace of GDP growth—will, generally speaking, be coming in below that pace of trend growth. So that's that gap between the 1.4 and the around two per cent. It's that gap that means that we reduce capacity pressures in the economy, the output gap moves to close, in economist parlance, and that brings inflation back down to around 2½ per cent, which is our target, obviously.

In terms of some of the differences with the Treasury team—and you spoke to them earlier—they are obviously far better placed than me to talk to their own forecasts, but there are just a couple that I would highlight. One is that, in terms of our productivity assumption, I think Treasury did outline earlier that over the forecast horizon we're talking about here, which is just the next two years, we're not so different in terms of productivity outcomes. But, on perhaps more of a medium-term basis, they do have a slightly higher rate of productivity growth than we do. Ours is an assumption that really anchors us for the two-year horizon, and it's 0.7 per cent year on year for labour productivity growth, but it is just a two-year assumption.

I'd also say that there are other differences around our assumptions for population growth. Again, we use the Centre for Population studies forecast, but we obviously used the prebudget numbers. We didn't have access to the budget numbers when we put these together. I understand there are a few differences there, and you can get a few other differences around labour supply more broadly.

But I think, really, it does come back in a very headline sense to the point the governor made earlier: different people can take a different view of what the outlook is going to look like. We do that. We do our forecasts independently, absolutely. We do talk to our colleagues in Treasury on a regular basis to discuss current conditions and the outlook at the moment. We're also discussing, clearly, the global outlook, which is really important right now. But the forecast teams in this particular case have slightly different profiles for GDP growth. But I would expect there to be differences. It would be very, very strange for us to completely agree all the time.

Senator CHANDLER: That being said, given that you will be making decisions based on your outlook, and fiscal policy decisions are being made on a slightly rosier outlook, are you concerned that this divergence between your view of the world and Treasury's view of the world may mean that monetary policy and fiscal policy are not working hand in hand to tackle inflation?

Ms Bullock: No, I'm not concerned about that. As I said, our focus is on inflation and keeping full employment, to the extent that we balance those two things. We just have to take fiscal policy as given, and we do. The extent to which our forecasts are slightly different from theirs plays out in a discussion at the board table, and board members are welcome to bring different views, and I can tell you different board members do bring different perspectives to the board table. So I'm not concerned that it hampers monetary policy at all.

CHAIR: Senator McKim.

Senator McKIM: Good afternoon, folks. Thanks for your time. Ms Bullock, you've made it clear that the latest round of interest rate rises was at least in significant part about ensuring that inflation expectations don't get embedded into the economy. Is that fair?

Ms Bullock: Yes, it is, but it's also—the key point that you didn't state was that it was in reaction to the fact that inflation was too high. It was a reflection of the fact that we had excess demand in the economy, and what you have to do in those circumstances is dampen demand, which, in our case, means raising interest rates because that's our instrument. If we don't do so, then there's a possibility it will get ingrained in inflation expectations. But the proximate issue here was excess demand in the economy.

Senator McKIM: When you say 'ensuring that inflation expectations don't get embedded', can I ask what you're actually referring to here, because, historically, that has been taken to mean workers demanding higher wages. Now, I'm going to assume that you're not concerned about a wage price spiral here and are potentially more concerned about firms that know they can take advantage of excess demand. Is that fair?

Ms Bullock: No, I don't think that's fair, Senator. I think what we're saying is that inflation expectations get ingrained in everyone's consciousness. So it's workers; it's firms. If everyone starts to think, 'You know what; the new normal is three or four per cent inflation,' workers think, 'Four per cent is good for wages,' and they're getting what inflation is delivering, and firms are putting up their prices by four per cent. So it's just inflation. That's what I'm talking about. It's not one set or the other; it's about everyone saying, 'You know what, inflation has been above three per cent for six years. The new normal is four per cent.' That's what I'm worried about.

Senator McKIM: Alright. Last month the RBA released its analysis of price-setting behaviour of firms during supply shocks. That analysis found 'a decline in price rigidity as firms became more willing to adjust prices'. It also found that that decline in price rigidity contributed meaningfully to the sharp rise in inflation in 2022 and 2023. Ms Bullock, I've previously asked you, in the context of the supply shocks caused by the COVID pandemic, whether you thought that—I'm quoting directly from my question here—'some firms or some sectors are using the cover of a significant rise in inflation and a lack of competition to boost their profits over and above what would be required to meet increases in their input costs'. Do you share the same concerns now, given the supply shocks that we're currently experiencing—that is, that some firms or some sectors in the economy are using the cover of these supply shocks and a lack of competition to boost their profits over and above what would be required to meet increases in their input costs?

Ms Bullock: You're talking about mark-ups and margins. In fact, we released a Bulletin article fairly recently about caution in interpreting increasing margins and inflation. So I would suggest you don't conflate increasing margins with inflation necessarily, because they can have different sorts of impacts, depending on the circumstances. Having said that—and I've said this before as well—firms can only put up their prices by more than their costs are inputting if, as you say, there is a competition issue. There might be a competition issue. But, in addition, they can only do it if demand allows them to do so. So, in circumstances where demand is running stronger than the economy can accommodate, then, yes, you can end up with firms putting up their prices by more because demand doesn't slow. The whole point about raising interest rates and trying to slow demand is to try and bring back that impetus for higher inflation.

I think it's easy to say that firms will just raise their prices by more than costs, but they can only do it if demand isn't impacted by that. Our judgment was, prior to the conflict in the Middle East and even then, that demand was running too strong for supply, and that's the reason why you could pass through cost increases—because demand was allowing you to do so.

Senator McKIM: Yes, I understand that point you're making, Ms Bullock, but can I ask again whether the RBA is concerned that firms, particularly firms in highly concentrated sectors of the economy, are using the cover of the current supply shocks that we are enduring to increase their prices over and above what would be required to meet increases in their input costs?

Ms Bullock: I have no evidence to make a comment on that, Senator. I have no evidence to suggest it is.

Senator McKIM: Can I ask this, then. Is the decline in price rigidity—that the RBA identified in its analysis of the price-setting behaviour of firms during supply shocks—more prevalent in highly concentrated sectors of the economy?

Dr Hunter : I'm happy to talk to that particular research paper. Just to reiterate what the governor said, I would encourage you to have a look at the Bulletin article that was released just last week because it does talk to this topic and has some empirical evidence that the governor just referred to. But that particular research paper wasn't looking at the degree of concentration in any particular sector. It was actually focused on the retail sector, because that's where we have access to new data that really allows us to dig into this question empirically in a way that we couldn't before. To understand how quickly prices are being reset, this paper makes use of effectively scanner data—individual products in the retail sector, looking at their pricing over time, and being able to strip out sales events and what have you. It's really detailed data, but it is just for that one sector, so it can't innately talk to the question that you're asking about.

I would also say that this particular paper was really looking at what the pricing response from businesses was through a period of time, which I'm sure you will remember, when we had substantial increases in costs going on. This was during COVID, where we had supply chain disruptions, and we had big shifts in the patterns of consumption across the global economy and here in Australia as well. So we had some products that were being imported, in many cases, where the prices were rising as rapidly as imported prices. This was really trying to get at how quickly our businesses are resetting their sales prices as a reflection of what's happening to their cost base. It wasn't really talking to a question of margins; it was really trying to get a handle on, in an environment where we've got costs moving quite rapidly—we're in another environment like that right now, of course, with the shock of the Middle East flowing through—what the firms do. So it wasn't really talking to the question you were asking. So it wasn't really talking to the question you were asking.

Senator McKIM: No, I understand that. That is, in fact, my point—that, although the circumstances are different, we are in a similar environment right now because of the illegal war that's being perpetrated on Iran by the US and Israel. But why wouldn't the RBA be interested in whether the decline in price rigidity that you identified stemming from the COVID period was more prevalent in highly concentrated sectors of the economy?

Dr Hunter : I wouldn't describe it as not being interested. As researchers and analysts and economists who are working in this space, we work with the information that we have and we dig into questions as we can. Again, I point you to the Bulletin article, which was looking at different data sources, not as high frequency—it can't draw the same conclusions, and we couldn't use the same empirical techniques on the data that that Bulletin article talks to, because it's just not as detailed—but it does talk to some of the questions that you are asking. To reiterate what the governor just said, in that paper you can see that, if you look at the different measures and metrics we have for margins and mark-ups—and they're not actually the same thing; they are used interchangeably but they're not the same thing—you can see that there aren't necessarily trends that we can identify in those data series by sector. But those data points and datasets are quite different. They're very aggregated. They don't let us dig down, certainly not to anything like the firm level, but they don't even let us dig down into what you might consider to be different sectors or industries within the economy. They are very high level. But the data is what it is and we do with it what we can.

This particular RDP was taking advantage of a new dataset that we've only just got access to. Of course, we want to expand our horizons and make use of new information, and this is one of the ways that we are trying to do that.

Senator McKIM: Ms Bullock, I'll go back to my previous questions about inflation expectations. I'll paraphrase you here, but you said that it's a range of matters that you're concerned about around the potential for inflation expectations to be embedded. As I pointed out, historically, that has been in significant part concerns about workers demanding higher wages. You're not seriously concerned about a wage price spiral here, are you?

Ms Bullock: No, I'm not. No.

Senator McKIM: Real wages are either stagnating or declining, depending on how far you want to go back, and workers basically just have to cop whatever they can get now. They don't have expectations of their real wages climbing anymore, because they just haven't for so long.

Ms Bullock: I said no. My answer is no.

Senator McKIM: You're not concerned—

Ms Bullock: I'm not concerned about a wage price spiral, no.

Senator McKIM: Alright, good.

CHAIR: Senator, two more minutes.

Senator McKIM: I'll just park it there because I've got another series of questions. I'll come back.

CHAIR: Senator Canavan.

Senator CANAVAN: Thank you, Governor. I note in your opening statement that you mentioned that you've increased the cash rate by 75 basis points this year. Was it a mistake to cut rates early last year?

Ms Bullock: No, I don't believe it was, and I don't believe the board thought it was. Circumstances changed, and when circumstances change, we have to change. I actually recall that, when we were gradually cutting rates through the first half of 2025, underlying inflation and headline inflation actually was back in the target band, the unemployment rate was rising, and we were copping a lot of flak for not cutting quickly enough. So, no, it wasn't a mistake.

Senator CANAVAN: If the inflation rate did break out earlier this year, before, as your opening statement notes, the Iran conflict, why did that happen?

Ms Bullock: What happened was that there was a slowing in demand, a little bit as interest rates came down, but also there was a rebound in demand, and particularly consumption, I think, rebounded a bit more than we thought. There were wealth effects coming through from the housing market, and things just rebounded more than we thought. The other thing was that the supply capacity in the economy was less than we thought it was, and so it didn't take much of a rebound in demand, which we saw through the second half of 2025, before it ran up against capacity constraints. That was why things started to move.

The other thing I would point out—and I pointed it out in the statement—is that, through the first half of 2025, you might recall that the trade issues with the United States were really front of mind for everyone. Everyone was really worried about the world economy. People were very uncertain. People were worried about what it might imply. As it turned out, through the second half of 2025—and it continues now—the AI boom in the United States has absolutely super charged everything. Many of our trading partners who were expecting to be very badly impacted by the trade restrictions and the tariffs weren't impacted nearly as much by those, and, in addition, they got a huge tailwind from AI. That's really helped us as well. So all of the circumstances that looked like we were deflating, we were seeing inflation come down and we were seeing activity slow and the world was seeing activity slow, all of a sudden, everything reversed. That goes for us and it goes for a number of other countries as well.

Senator CANAVAN: In your answer just there, you said that the supply capacity of the economy was 'less than we thought' and that things 'rebounded more than we thought'. If your thoughts were wrong, didn't you make a mistake in cutting interest rates last year?

Ms Bullock: I don't believe we did. I think we were doing the right thing at the right time. We were trying to be forward looking in looking at what was happening into the data and where our forecasts were leading us. As I said, if you recall, the views about the Australian economy and the world economy in that period when the trade tensions were going on was very, very poor. Everyone was downgrading their forecasts; everyone was worried. What ended up happening was, of course, that the tariffs didn't end up being anywhere near as bad as everyone thought to begin with, so a whole lot of things changed. Forecasts can't take into account these sorts of things. We know we're in uncertain times. We're in new uncertain times now. Forecasts are difficult. We have to do them because we can't be backward looking. But, if it turns out that the forecasts are changed because of external factors or because perhaps they weren't quite right in the first place, then you change—and that's what we did.

Senator CANAVAN: Yes, that's right. Yogi Berra is right about forecasts. But I thought, at least in part, the reason why we appoint people with expertise to the RBA board, and yourself, is to look into the future to make predictions. There's nothing wrong with getting it wrong, but I think your evidence today indicates you got it wrong and, therefore, you made a mistake. I'm not so concerned about you making mistakes; I'm more concerned about you not being able to admit to it. That concerns me more greatly. If you've made a mistake in your forecasts, haven't you made a mistake in your decision?

Ms Bullock: One has got to make forecasts, otherwise one is looking in the rear view mirror, and everyone with hindsight can say you made a mistake. So, no, I don't accept we made a mistake. In fact, I think that, if we hadn't have been lowering interest rates at the time, if things had turned out differently with respect to the trade restrictions and so on, if we hadn't have been lowering, people would have been screaming at us, 'Why weren't you!' So, no, I don't accept we made a mistake. We work with what we've got. We have to make forecasts. We know they're not perfect, but we have to do them and we have to act on the basis of what we think is our best guess. We do do scenarios to try and get a feel for where the risks lie, and, in those circumstances back then, where we saw the risk lying was more on the downside. It turns out, we had changes that meant this came up on the upside, so we changed.

Senator CANAVAN: I'll just move to a different topic. We saw in yesterday's national accounts another disappointing result for productivity. Productivity has now been negative for over four years. It has never been anything like this in recorded history. How concerned are you about our productivity performance and how it might restrain your decisions and their impact on potential inflation?

Ms Bullock: Well, yes, concerned, and (b) we can't grow any quicker than supply side allows us. And you can't get any growth in real incomes if you don't have productivity growth. But that's not something we can control. All we can do is set policy appropriately.

Senator CANAVAN: It was the issue last year, when you lowered interest rates, and, as you say, the supply capacity of the economy was less than we thought. Is part of the reason for that lack of capacity in supply our poor productivity performance?

Ms Bullock: Yes.

Dr Hunter : I can probably provide a bit more detail on that. If you go back to our August Statement on monetary policy, you will see in there that there's a special chapter on productivity. In that, we outlined our recent performance and effectively built up why we were, at that point, downgrading our medium-term assumption for productivity growth from one per cent—that's labour productivity growth, sorry—a year to 0.7 per cent a year. That's the assumption that sort of anchors the back end of our forecast, if you like. So we were only looking at a two- to three-year forecast horizon, but we do, as the governor has just said, have to take an assumption on that because we need to think about how fast the economy can grow, and productivity growth is obviously a really important part of that. So, in August last year, we actually published that piece of work and incorporated that new judgment, or new assumption, if you like, into the forecast. We haven't changed it since, so we've held that through to where we are today.

I would also like to say that, in terms of the productivity performance for the March quarter specifically—we have said this before, but I do think it's worth saying again—we wouldn't really look quarter to quarter at productivity outcomes. They're very volatile. They can be knocked around by all sorts of one-off temporary factors, so we don't typically look quarter to quarter. In fact, we were anticipating prior to yesterday's data that we might get a decline on the quarter in productivity as a mechanical outcome from what we saw of labour market outcomes and what we expected to see for GDP, because those two things, broadly speaking, came in line with our expectation. We weren't surprised by what we got yesterday. But I would certainly point you to that August SMP special chapter so that you can see and read more of our views on productivity.

CHAIR: Eight minutes, Senator.

Senator CANAVAN: Thank you. The Statement on monetary policy has a forecast productivity growth rate of zero per cent for the June 2026 quarter. I was a little confused by the heading of that table. Is that a year on year or a quarter-on-quarter growth rate?

Dr Hunter : That would be a year-on-year number. For us, labour productivity is output from the non-farm sector per hour worked, so we strip out agriculture, effectively, because that, as I'm sure you are very aware, gets knocked around by weather and other events that really are random. We don't tend to focus too much on that; we take that out. And we're looking on a per hour worked basis because that's our measure for labour input into the economy.

Senator CANAVAN: I think we took evidence earlier that the Treasury is forecasting a productivity growth rate of 1.2 per cent. That seems way above yours, though, so what's the reason for the difference?

Dr Hunter : I don't have the Treasury numbers to hand, and I'm not sure if that was their assumption for the medium- to long-term productivity growth rate. That would be, I think, their five- to 10-year assumption. I don't know what they're forecasting for the June quarter specifically, but I do know that their forecasting and ours are not so different for the June quarter, so I would be surprised if they are very different, but you would have to take that up with them.

Senator CANAVAN: Are you concerned then that, with this low productivity performance and another energy crisis which the International Energy Agency says is the worst since the 1970s, we are at risk of entering a period of stagflation?

Ms Bullock: It depends on what you define as stagflation. What I can say is that we are seeing the trade-off between inflation and growth go the wrong way and between inflation and unemployment go the wrong way. So, for every level of unemployment, what we are experiencing is higher inflation. That's not a good thing, obviously, because, as I said earlier, inflation is bad for everyone in the economy. And that's why, as I was answering Senator McKim, I was making the point that we want to make sure this is a one-off lift in the price level and not embedded into expectations about continual rises of this nature. That's the key.

Senator CANAVAN: Okay.

CHAIR: I'm going to rotate the call. Senator Bragg.

Senator BRAGG: Thanks very much. I want to ask you a few questions, firstly, about the five per cent deposit scheme. Do you have any concerns about the way that the scheme may be impacting house prices or increasing prudential risk in the system?

Ms Bullock: No, we have no concerns, I don't think, about increasing prudential risk in the financial system. We have observed that there has been an increase in the first home buyer interest. I think we have seen a lift in that and in credit to first home buyers. We have also seen an increase in the loan-to-valuation ratios reflecting that. But we don't have any concerns that that's in any way threatening financial stability.

Senator BRAGG: Have you had any input into the deployment of APRA's macroprudential tools to rein in risky lending at some level?

Ms Bullock: The way it works, Senator, is that the Reserve Bank provides advice to APRA, or the Reserve Bank—sorry, I should say the Monetary Policy Board provides advice once a year to APRA on where it sees the financial stability risks. Then APRA take that and they make decisions on their macroprudential policy. We do not tell them what to do with macroprudential policy. We provide them with the analytical input about financial stability risks, and then they decide whether or not they will take action and, if so, what they will do.

Senator BRAGG: Have you given any thought to the risk of people going into negative equity?

Ms Bullock: That is something that our financial stability team do look at. At the moment, practically no-one is in negative equity. Negative equity matters if people get into trouble with their loans and then they have to sell their homes to meet that. That's why a strong employment market at the moment is really important, because when people have employment—the things that end up with people having to sell in distressed circumstances are often loss of employment, family break-ups and those sorts of things. So, at the moment, if you look at negative equity, though, it's absolutely miniscule. It's not big at all.

Senator BRAGG: What sort of forward projections are your internal analysts imagining might—are you doing scenario planning?

Ms Bullock: We do scenarios. In our Financial stability review we often do scenarios about what sorts of things would result in large increases in negative equity. We also do some work on looking at households that are—in effect, we try to do estimates of the percentage of households that are paying out more in mortgage repayments than they have spare income, disposable income. That's fairly small, and it has actually declined over the last year or so. So we do these sorts of scenarios. But I have to say that, because of the increase in the house prices over the last few years, as I said earlier, negative equity is a very small share of loans.

Senator BRAGG: I want to take you to an FOI that has recently been released from the bank which talks about some of your internal deliberation on housing policy. Am I right in saying that, in relation to dwelling investment, that goes negative from 2027 under your projections?

Dr Hunter : Yes. The negative number is the growth rate in dwelling investment activity as captured by the national accounts. So, yes, you are right. We have positive year on year through the first half of the forecast horizon, roughly speaking, and then we tip and have some negative. That would be the level of activity dropping from where it gets to. So it's a cycle, if you like. It's a bit of a humped shape profile for the level of activity.

Senator BRAGG: So according to your projections the Housing Accord won't be met, will it?

Dr Hunter : We actually discussed this, I think, around a month or so ago at a separate hearing. We don't on a regular basis do forecasts for dwelling completions. And that's certainly the case today. We haven't done a forecast of dwelling completions. That is consistent with our May SMP forecast. What we do have is a housing market and rental market model that works on a sort of approvals, completions, number of dwellings basis, if you like. We use that to really dig into housing market dynamics. We can look at what that model would say about how dwelling approvals and what have you could evolve. But, because it's not part of our core forecast framework, we don't do those forecasts on a regular basis. So I can't tell you what our current dwelling investment forecast profile means for completions, because we haven't done that work.

Senator BRAGG: Page 6 of this FOI says:

The annual completions implied by our forecasts remain below the National Housing Accord targets (including the original 1 million target) and previous peaks.

The target is 1.2 million.

Dr Hunter : Yes. It is certainly true that the latest dwelling completions number, if you just annualise that, is running below what would be consistent with building 1.2 million homes over five years. That's true and a statement about the historical data, but what I can't tell you is what our current forecasts imply for future completions, because we haven't done that work.

Senator BRAGG: I understand that, but your current analysis as released under FOI—

Dr Hunter : That analysis was from, I think, around a year or so ago. I would have to check the date, so I can't confirm that, but I think that it was dated from around then.

Senator BRAGG: Okay. But, as a reasonable person looking at these documents, you would assume that your view is that, just as the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council says, we won't hit the accord target of 1.2 million houses.

Ms Bullock: I think Sarah has already said that we have no forecasts on that. That may well be the case, but that is not our job.

Senator BRAGG: Okay.

Ms Bullock: Our job is to keep inflation low and stable, and the best thing we can do to help the housing market is to make sure we keep inflation low and stable. That's the best thing we can do.

Senator BRAGG: I understand your job is to fight inflation, and we wish you well in that endeavour of course. It's a very difficult challenge. But it does say in this document that you have forecasts.

Dr Hunter : As I said, we have a separate model. It's the Tulip and Saunders model. That's named after a couple of people who used to work at the bank who actually developed the thing in the mid to late 2010s.

Senator BRAGG: They are very famous.

Dr Hunter : Very famous. It is used right across the country and it is a benchmark model. So we have that. As I said, what we really primarily use that model and that model framework for is looking at housing market dynamics. It helps us to understand how prices, rents and vacancy rates might evolve—these important features of the housing market. As the governor said earlier, we are interested in the housing market because it is an important transmission channel for monetary policy. It is also an important sector in the economy full stop, and it's rightly getting the attention that it needs. But we don't use it as part of our core forecasting framework. What we are really interested in the context of inflation is the amount of activity that's happening in the economy. With respect to housing, that activity is broader than just dwelling completions. It includes alterations and additions, for example. It's important what type of housing is being built—a detached dwelling versus an attached medium-high density. All of that detail and richness really gets aggregated up for us in the national accounts framework and dwelling investment series. That's the real focus for our forecast. So that's why we focus our attention there. That ultimately is what really matters for inflation outcomes for that balance of demand and supply that the governor was talking about earlier on.

Senator BRAGG: As per these documents, your forecasts suggest that we won't get to 1.2 million. Have your forecasts changed since these documents were prepared internally?

Ms Bullock: I think that's what Sarah is saying.

Dr Hunter : Yes, they have. The forecasts are updated once a quarter. The core forecasts are updated once a quarter and released in the SMP. As I said, I would have to go away and check the dates on these documents and on those particular numbers. But they are not from May 2026, so they are not consistent with our latest forecast. So, yes, the forecasts change.

CHAIR: You are at nine minutes, Senator Bragg.

Senator BRAGG: Can you get those to us on notice.

Dr Hunter : The dates for these documents? Yes, I think we can provide those to you.

Senator BRAGG: Staying with these documents for a second, what about the issue of migration in housing policy? You say, 'How does government influence the housing market,' and you list tax and migration. How in your mind does migration affect housing policy in Australia?

Dr Hunter : Those points being called out were really highlighting, if you like, the fundamental drivers for housing demand and housing supply—structural features of the economy. Just starting on the demand side, that's where migration comes in. So, ultimately, demand for housing is the number of households that are forming in the economy, and that's really a function of three things: the natural increase in the population, which is births minus deaths, to be very crude, and I'm sorry for that; net migration, which is people that are moving here minus the people that are leaving; and average household size, which is how many households are formed out of that total resident population. All that that document is really highlighting with respect to migration policy is that obviously the migration policy settings have an impact on the number of people that migrate to Australia, so that then comes through in the population numbers. It was really just saying that. It was almost a mechanical statement about what the drivers are of housing demand, ultimately, and obviously that comes back to population.

CHAIR: Last question, Senator Bragg.

Senator BRAGG: Does migration add to housing demand?

Dr Hunter : A growing population increases demand for housing, and migration is part of that, yes. But really what matters ultimately, certainly for us in thinking about inflation and monetary policy setting, is the interaction of demand with housing supply. For instance, as an empirical sort of observation from history, Australia, generally speaking, has built and completed more dwellings per person than other countries with slower population growth. That's a supplier response to demand. So we are really interested in both sides of the equation, not just one side, and that's indeed why the document that you are referring to calls out features that are reflective of the supply side of the equation rather than demand, which will be the tax settings and the regulatory settings.

Senator BRAGG: Thanks. I just have one more and then I'm done. The other point on that page is that you indicated the tax settings could be a factor. What do you say about the significant tax changes to housing and to CGT? How does that affect housing, do you think?

Dr Hunter : We are obviously still digesting those, as I think everybody is, and we will be looking at how they come through in the established housing market, and then over time we will looking at how they come through into approvals. But we haven't got any analysis that we can provide to you at this stage. They are very new. I guess what we can say is what we hear from some of the banks and other contacts that we talk to is that the tax changes do seem to be having some impact in the established dwellings market. That's not unexpected; I think the Treasury analysis that was put out as part of the budget also anticipated that. But I can't give you any more than that. It's very new, so I'm not sure.

Ms Bullock: It's new. In the past, when we have done work on this, we thought it would impact investor demand. That might mean that it's easier for first home buyers to get into the market. You might recall that, back in 2014 and 2017, when APRA put restrictions on first interest-only loans and investor loans, investor lending came up or owner-occupier lending came up, including first home buyers. So it might mean that there's a bit of a change in the mix of housing. What it does eventually in the long run I don't think we necessarily know; it's a bit uncertain. But one expectation, certainly from our work in the past and just some observations relative to 2014 and 2017, is that if investor demand does come up, you might see a switch.

CHAIR: Thank you. Senator McKim, I think you are going to share your block with Senator Pocock.

Senator McKIM: I am indeed, Chair. Ms Bullock, there has been more discussion about stagflation recently than there has been for some time. Has the Reserve Bank seen any indication that the global economy is heading into a period of low growth, rising unemployment and rising inflation?

Ms Bullock: The first thing I would say is that this has been a massive supply shock, and when we get supply shocks what happens is that, as I said earlier, the trade off between unemployment and inflation worsens. That's what happens. The key, though—and this is what you will hear central banks around the world talking about—is that, with supply shocks, there is some ability to look through the initial direct impact. The central banks are very focused on making sure that there are not second-round effects—that the price level change, because of the supply shock, doesn't turn into a consistent inflation shock. I don't think anyone thinks that there is stagflation going on around the world at the moment. I think what central banks are being very focused on is making sure that we don't end up in a situation where we have permanently higher inflation. That's what central banks are focused on.

Senator McKIM: As part of the discussion, CBA's economics team under Luke Yeaman have made a distinction that we are experiencing an impulse of stagflation but not yet a drawn-out persistent episode. Of course, that kind of episode would require prolonged inflation, a feedback loop between rising wages and prices, and higher inflation expectations locking in. Would you agree that we are experiencing an impulse of stagflation?

Ms Bullock: No, I wouldn't even use the term 'stagflation' in the current circumstance. I think we are in a supply shock. Stagflation is about their second point, which is about a prolonged period of high inflation and very poor growth and poor employment outcomes. We're not in that situation.

Senator McKIM: You went to this a little bit in your opening statement, but there's going to be lag effects to the supply shock that we're currently undergoing, sort of second-round inflation effects—sorry, I'm using lay terms here—to everything from food to anything that needs to be moved around by vehicles or boats. Do you not think that those circumstances are potentially a precursor to a stagflationary episode?

Ms Bullock: It goes back exactly to what we were talking about before, which is making sure that people see this as a pricing level shift and not a shift in the level of inflation, and that's where inflation expectations come in. So we need to make sure that, to the extent that the price of fuel has gone up and it stays there—that has introduced a permanent cost increase to many industries as well, so they will put that into their prices, but there it should stop. But, if it gets into inflation expectations, it won't stop, and that's the whole point. You have got to constrain it to a price level. When central banks are talking about second-round effects here, they are talking about the possibility of the second-round effects of this getting embedded into people's psyche, and then you end up with inflation expectations adjusting. In our inflation forecast, that's what we've got embedded in there—the fact that there is going to be flow-on effects to industries and firms that use products that are impacted by the fuel price rise.

Dr Kent : Can I just add something?

Ms Bullock : Yes.

Dr Kent : Globally, markets are thinking that, yes, inflation will be higher in the next one, two or three years but, much further out beyond that, not persistently higher. Inflation expectations from a range of measures and the longer term, five to 10 years out, are very consistent with inflation targets. Part of that is because central banks are expected to respond. We've responded; the Norwegian Central Bank has responded. I would argue the Fed has responded by not cutting rates, which they were widely expected to have done of late, and others are expected to be raising rates a bit. Whether that's sufficient or not, time will tell. But I think that says there is not a widespread expectation of stagflation—that is, persistently high inflation. That doesn't mean there won't a period of some higher inflation and some weaker growth for a time. But beyond the next year or two, markets and economists globally are not looking for that. That doesn't mean there couldn't be further pressures if the supply shock worsens. But central banks are expected to have learnt the lessons of stagflation of the seventies and to get on top of it.

Ms Bullock: It's worth pointing out that if central banks don't respond that's when expectations will start to move.

Senator McKIM: Yes. It's a very uncertain world that we live in at the moment, and assumptions can vary wildly in terms of the potential for supply shocks, new supply shocks or extensions of existing supply shocks. But I have a last question on stagflation. The deputy governor, Mr Hauser, recently described stagflation as 'a central banker's nightmare'. Is that because, ultimately, if the world is heading into a period of stagflation, whether it's an impulse or a persistent episode, that central banks need to basically choose between inflation and a recession?

Ms Bullock: The reason I think it's a nightmare is that we have a dual mandate. But it does mean, as we saw from the seventies, if you are going to get inflation back down from high levels—and I have to say, we are still only in the threes and fours here; we are not in the 17s in inflation. But, if inflation does get higher and you end up in this very severe period of stagflation, the only way to get it down is to increase interest rates substantially, and that is likely to mean a very bad growth outcome and potentially recession. So we don't want to go there.

Senator McKIM: Thanks. I appreciate your willingness to engage in that discussion, and I will ask Senator Pocock to fill in the rest of the block.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you. I have a couple of questions about KPMG. Do KPMG play any role in the audit of the bank?

Ms Bullock: Yes, they do, but we don't have a direct relationship with them. We have a relationship with the ANAO, and the ANAO engages an auditor, and they have engaged KPMG.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: What is the actual reality of that relationship? KPMG staff are looking at the detail of your audit?

Ms Bullock: Yes. KPMG do the audit, and they are engaged by ANAO to do the audit of the financial statements, and they're focused on the financial statements.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: We have been reading about your whistleblower hotline contract with KPMG, the one called Fair Call. Have you had any contact with KPMG about that in recent days?

Ms Bullock: Yes, we are going to be re-tendering for it.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: What was the value and length of that contract, historically?

Ms Bullock: I don't know the length. I know the value was about $10,000 a year.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Have you got any other contracts with KPMG?

Ms Bullock: Yes, we have had a contract with KPMG where they have done some work for us on immigration. Sometimes when we are bringing staff in from overseas, foreign staff, we've had a contract with them for assistance in—I'm not familiar with what you have to do, but there's quite a process you have to go through to bring in staff from overseas. They assist with that. That contract is also out for tender.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Given the open discussion, the concessions by KPMG in recent days about their misdemeanours—their unethical use of information to win contracts, their treatment of their whistleblower and use of AI to cheat in exams—what is the bank's view about contracting in the future with KPMG?

Ms Bullock: I think we will be looking very closely at it. I don't think we'll be reappointing them to the whistleblower service. We are re-tendering for that. In terms of the audit, that is a matter for the ANAO, and you had better speak to the Auditor-General about that.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thanks for those answers.

CHAIR: We'll go to Senator Smith.

Senator DEAN SMITH: Thank you very much for your participation this afternoon. Can you update the committee on what the bank's liaison program is observing with regard to how community services, charities and not-for-profit organisations might be responding to increased cost-of-living pressures being experienced by Australian families?

Ms Bullock: Sarah might have some more recent information, but, at a general level over the last couple of years, I would have to say generally when we speak to not-for-profits and charities, they have expressed the view that they are seeing a heightened level of demand from households and often from households that they wouldn't necessarily expected to have seen from in the past. This even persisted, I think, when interest rates were going down. So it's not actually necessarily an interest rate story; it's a cost-of-living story. It's about prices of things. The unfortunate thing is that, when we talk about bringing inflation down, we are talking about bringing down the rate at which prices are rising. We are not talking about bringing prices down. So what people are suffering is the fact that prices are just much higher than they were a few years ago. That's the general sort of flavour we get from them.

I myself have done a couple of sessions with our liaison team, speaking to charities and speaking to debt hotlines and those sorts of things, and it's a very similar story that I hear personally, which is that demand is heightened and that things that are worrying people are the prices of the goods and services that they have to buy and their essentials.

Dr Hunter : I would just add to that. I met with an organisation very recently, within the last month or so, and it's clearly a very challenging time for some members of our community. There is no hiding away from that, and some people really are struggling. They were saying that just in the last couple of months, so more or less since the conflict in the Middle East has broken out—and obviously that's come through into higher fuel prices in particular, but it's starting to show up in other parts of the economy—they are seeing, if anything, more demand for their services. It goes with what the governor was just saying, that obviously that is clearly a sign of cost-of-living pressures that have intensified in recent months. That's not surprising for us to hear, but it's clearly really challenging for the community and for certain members. Bringing the cost-of-living increases back down to manageable levels is clearly something that we hear a lot that is really important to this particular group.

You know, generally if you are managing on fixed incomes, if you are struggling with that, then having certainty of what things are going to cost when you go to the shops or fill your car up and what have you is a really important part of how you have security, and that's a really strong message that we get from the liaison program in these areas.

Senator DEAN SMITH: What variation are you seeing between capital cities?

Dr Hunter : Generally speaking, it's actually, I would say, perhaps a bit more of a reflection of what we see across the whole economy. What we can see if we look at even just labour market data and some of the survey data and things, is that, generally speaking, conditions in Victoria—Melbourne, specifically—are a bit more challenging than in other parts of the country. You can see that in the labour market outcomes. The unemployment rate there, generally speaking, is a touch higher, though it can jump from month to month. At the other end of the scale, if you like, we are generally seeing stronger outcomes in terms of the labour market activity more broadly in Western Australia, so obviously Perth; Adelaide in South Australia; and up in Queensland. Actually the Queensland story is not just a Brisbane story. We're hearing that from other parts of the state as well. It's not atypical for the country to be going at different speeds in different geographies and regions. It just so happens that that's the distribution at the moment and that it's the larger cities, particularly Melbourne, that are perhaps a bit softer than some of the other cities.

Senator DEAN SMITH: In your opening statement, you do acknowledge that it is a difficult time for many households facing cost-of-living pressures. At a household level, how are Australian families responding to the cost-of-living pressures?

Ms Bullock : We don't have really granular data on individual households. What we can observe—and we do a little bit of this through our Financial stability review. You might recall earlier I was talking about how we do try to get some estimates of the extent to which households are spending more than they've got in disposable income. We do try to get a handle on that. It's a relatively small share of population, less than five per cent of households, but for those households it's absolutely devastating and critical. In saying it's a small proportion, I'm not suggesting that it's a great outcome; it's not. So we can do that sort of work.

There's more aggregate data that looks at household balance sheets more broadly. I'll ask Chris to talk very briefly about the way mortgage holders are handling some of these things. But generally, if you look at coming out of the pandemic and the government assistance through the pandemic, many households—not all, as some really struggled, but many—came out with a household balance sheet that looked a lot stronger than it did. From an aggregate perspective, the household balance sheets have looked pretty strong. Some evidence of that comes from the way that we observe people treat their mortgages. I might just get Chris to say a couple of words on that.

Dr Kent : Coming out of the pandemic, as Michele said, many households—by absolutely no means all—had substantial savings. That makes a lot of sense because they were still receiving income but, in many cases, were in lockdown and couldn't travel overseas and spend that money on holidays and so on. Spending was severely curtailed. The other thing, though, is that, unlike in an economy like the US, they typically didn't go and then spend those, whereas that buffer of savings out of the pandemic for the household sector in the US was largely spent within a few years. That was not the case in Australia.

The other feature of that is that, for those who had mortgages, they tended to maintain quite a lot of extra payments, so that's paying more than the bank requires you to pay contractually every fortnight or every month. That was even ramped up a little bit more, not surprisingly, when we raised interest rates, because at high interest rates all households, including those with a mortgage, have an incentive to pay down their debts or save more. Those extra payments have been sustained for quite some time and are still holding up. That does not say that that's the case for all households or all mortgage holders. What I'm saying is for the household sector as a whole and for mortgage holders as a whole, or the average mortgage holder if you like, but there are mortgage holders who are obviously struggling to make their payments. That's always true, but those numbers are pretty low in the scheme.

Senator DEAN SMITH: With rising inflation and, as a consequence, increasing interest rates, there must be an erosion to that buffer of savings that you have reflected on. Secondly, how do you record what that erosion rate might be?

Dr Kent : We can look at the episode of higher inflation from 2022 onwards as a good example of what might happen now, and that's perhaps a surprising thing to many people. Yes, households are under cash-flow pressures, and many who do have savings buffers have to fall back on those and rely on them to help support consumption in the face of higher interest payments if they have a mortgage—particularly if they've lost a job, which makes things very stressful. Some, unfortunately, are forced off and sell their house. But, in the main, the average mortgage holder was actually maintaining those savings buffers. So what they were doing was cutting back on consumption. That's one of the key mechanisms through which monetary policy works—not just the cash-flow channel but the decisions that households make, when they can afford to, to maintain savings rates and even increase them. That's what economists would call the intertemporal savings channel of monetary policy.

Senator DEAN SMITH: In the governor's opening statement, she says, 'We expect the unemployment rate to increase over the coming year.' Surely, if that is to be realised, rising levels of unemployment is the point at which people feeling a degree of comfort—not the right word—in terms of being able to manage cost-of-living pressures, shifts to anxiety. This is particularly the situation in Western Australia, where people, I think it's fair to say, have an expectation of job choices in addition to the job that they've got. Once the risk of losing a job, or just the reduction in job choices, becomes more apparent to them than the level of anxiety around the cost of living, it really does start to tick up.

Dr Kent : Absolutely. What those households will often do is rein in their consumption to make sure they're still putting away for a rainy day in case they are one of those people who, for a length of time, is out of work.

Dr Hunter : Just to add to that, we saw the consumer confidence series decline very sharply at the start of the conflict. They've come back up a little bit but not all the way since, as it's become clear that perhaps the terrible, terrible outcomes are not yet true. But one of our main questions at the moment, in the context of the outlook, is: how does that shift in confidence impact that channel? It's exactly as you're talking about. How does that show up in consumer spending and in those decisions that Chris was just talking about? We're very actively looking at that at the moment. You're absolutely right. It is a really important transmission channel through the economy, and we're very alive to and looking very closely at it right at this moment.

Ms Bullock : Yes. It's not clear exactly how much impact we'll have, because there's not a great relationship. But, then, this is a very big drop in consumer confidence, so it could have some impact.

Senator DEAN SMITH: Thank you. If time allows can we come back to me?

CHAIR: Yes. Senator Chandler.

Senator CHANDLER: I want to circle back to some comments, Governor, that you made earlier. We were talking about the impact that the budget has had. Now, I am not in a position to say what level of public demand is an appropriate level of public demand. That is a matter for the parliament and the government to decide. I take it as given. Senator CHANDLER: So, as you foreshadowed, the Reserve Bank is doing something here in terms of fiscal policy—obviously. Ms Bullock : You can see that in the forecast table, Senator. You can see that growth in real wages—both measures that we have in there—declines to the end of this year, but then starts growing again.

Senator CHANDLER: Okay.

Ms Bullock : That's that hump in inflation.

Senator CHANDLER: Given this and, given the initial question I asked regarding the impact of the budget, I'll just ask one more time: is this budget making it easier for you to lower aggregate demand or does it do nothing to change it? If it does nothing to change it, that's not still particularly useful, is it?

Ms Bullock : In terms of where we thought we were in our May forecast, which is where we are here, the budget doesn't look different enough to change the impact of public demand on aggregate demand. Now, mathematically, if you said to me, 'If public demand was lower, would aggregate demand be lower?' I'd say, 'Yes, it would be, if private demand didn't rise.' I don't know the answer to that question. You could lower public demand, but you'd decrease expenditure and services and all these sorts of things. Yes, you could do that, but I don't know what would happen to private demand. If private demand didn't respond, then we'd end up basically in a situation where we'd have much lower growth.

This is the challenge. It's not just one or the other. We've got to think about it in terms of the total, and, mathematically, private and public add up to aggregate. You can't just say, 'Lower public demand,' because you don't know what's happening to the rest of it.

Senator CHANDLER: But one is more within the government's control than the other.

Ms Bullock : The government controls fiscal policy, yes, and it can change public demand. All I'm saying is that we take it as given, and it's not for me to tell the government what to do with fiscal policy.

Senator CHANDLER: Just on the public demand forecasts, how certain are you of them? I'm interested in understanding how recent outcomes have compared to what the RBA has forecast in relation to public demand.

To your question on public demand and forecast revisions, I would reiterate what the governor said earlier: forecasts are innately uncertain. Inevitably, somewhere in this table, multiple numbers will be wrong once we get actuals, so our forecasts are not perfect by any stretch.

But in terms of how we put together the forecast for public demand, what we do is take the budgets, federal and state, together, obviously, then, taking account of what's actually legislated and whether there are any changes that we have to be aware of there. We take them, we convert them into quarterly numbers, we map them across into current consumption, investment and so on, and we aggregate them up. One of the things that we do through that process is take account of what has happened historically to actual public demand, as measured by the ABS, relative to what was implied by the aggregation of those budgets, and we make an adjustment for that forecast error, if you like.

So we are trying to get ahead of at least one possible area where the forecast might be wrong. But are these forecasts more or less certain than other components in the table? No. Forecasting is innately hard. That's true for that particular line item. It's true for all of the line items in here.

Senator CHANDLER: So, just in summary, have you been underestimating the strength of public demand in recent quarters?

Ms Bullock : No.

Dr Hunter : No, not in general. That was a specific reference to the March quarter data that we got yesterday, and it was a relatively small difference as well. So I would say that, in a broad sense, no, we weren't particularly surprised by that.

Ms Bullock : Basically, we—

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry—in quarters before the March quarter?

Senator CANAVAN: I want to ask a little bit about the data centre situation. There's been some commentary in the past day that, if not for investment in data centres, we'd all be ruined. Is it having another impact on, say, the net-imports account, given that, presumably, much of the material that goes into making data centres is something we have to import. Is that something you've looked at?

Ms Bullock : The answer to your question is yes. We think there is a big offset in the import side of things because we import a lot of that equipment. There is some that will be domestic. Obviously, they've got to construct buildings to put all the equipment in and so on. But there is a big offset in the import side of things.

Senator CANAVAN: Have you looked at it in a quantitative sense at this stage?

Dr Hunter : Again, just in reference to yesterday's data because it is very timely—what we saw in yesterday's data was a substantial increase in private machinery and equipment investment, and, within that, it was the category that's associated with data centres. It's IT equipment, server-rack servers and what have you.

As the governor just said, we saw it coming through on the demand side within business investment, but we also saw it coming through in the equivalent category on the import side. Those two things do net-off in a GDP sense. What adds to GDP is, as the governor was just saying, the activity of building the shed—I'm told from the sector is the right lingo—and installing the actual equipment where that requires tradespeople, electricians in particular, to do that work.

That installation and building activity counts as part of our GDP. That's done domestically. But, when the equipment is imported, it offsets what shows up on the investment side.

Senator CANAVAN: What about the long-term impacts? Is that something you're looking at now?
