Dr Hunter : What we are looking at, and I'm sure lots of other people are as well, is, in particular, the rollout of AI technologies into workplaces—what that might do in the context of productivity, how it might change how different firms and institutions operate, and then what that might mean in the context of demand for different types of skills and expertise in the labour market. We're certainly considering that.

To your question around what types of services Australia imports, and thinking about IT services as an import category, it certainly is in there. We certainly track it as part of imports. Our models do have a dynamic and a relationship that links back demand to those import channels.

Secondly, we do, as standard, and have done for some time—AI obviously is a relatively new piece of work for us to be starting to undertake, but it is something that we're now actively researching.

Senator CANAVAN: Just turning to the fuel crisis—have you at all looked at the rundown in oil reserves in our region? Some new data has just popped up for me today, although this is, I think, a commonly reported on issue. China's oil imports have plunged by 38 per cent compared to the previous year. They're importing just 6.6 million barrels a day. They were well over 10 million barrels a day for most of the past year. It's obviously huge. It's generally thought that the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz is something like 12 to 14 million barrels a day, and there's other ways it can get out. That change in China's imports alone provides enormous relief.

Have you done any analysis of how sustainable this is? Are we somewhat not seeing as much of a crisis as was feared because of a rundown of reserves? Obviously, that has a limited life, as a strategy, if the crisis continues.

Ms Bullock : We don't do this independently. We get some information from Treasury and the government on what they're seeing in this space. I think Jenny Wilkinson addressed this issue in her appearance before the Senate. We have seen oil prices increase a lot, but they could have increased a lot more. There are two reasons for that. One is that there's been a bit of a response from the US oil producers in particular and a bit more supply from there. Around the world, not just in China, everyone is running down their reserves. There is a question about when we get to a point where that is no longer providing support to the oil market, and I think that is something that's front of mind for many countries. I'm not sure what that timeframe is. We're getting our information from Treasury, and they're hooked into the government on this. That's something that everyone is very focused on.

Senator CANAVAN: On another impact of this fuel crisis, there was a report yesterday that wheat crop in Australia could be down by up to 50 per cent. Ms Bullock : I think the answer is yes. I don't know if we've got firm estimates yet, but it's something that we're focused on.

We're looking at it in the context of production, as you mentioned. We would expect that to ultimately come through in food prices. That's actually an example of what the governor was talking about earlier—how those indirect effects can take time to show up—but we know that they're coming. We've had the very immediate direct effect from higher petrol and diesel prices that you put in your car. What we know is that, down the track, there are likely to be these further indirect effects. One example is that higher food cost flows through into the supply chain and ultimately into the price consumers have to pay when they go to the shops.

Ms Kelly : As Mr Kelly said, we have gone to the CFR, as part of the Economic Reform Roundtable, to get a whole bunch of ideas around where regulatory burden could be relieved. Senator HUME: You can probably see where I'm going with this. Senator HUME: Where will it be reported?

Senator HUME: Yes. When you've done that, where will we see that reported?

Senator HUME: Okay.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: To make sure I understand the nature of the reports: after this, an options paper was developed and then subsequently a further paper, neither of them released, which canvassed what the next steps might be around those options. Is that correct?

Mr Quinlivan : We've continued to do work on what options could look like in a more detailed way. That more detailed work hasn't fed into a paper.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Is there a plan to release that more detailed work? Can you take on notice providing that material to us.

Mr Quinlivan : I can take that on notice.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I want to go to tax issues. A large corporation is taxed at around 30 per cent around our country. However, income tax arrangements for the big four are very, very different. It's usually paid out as income to partners—income splitting is often a feature of the way partners handle their income—splitting it with partners, the use of Everett assignments and service trusts to minimise tax. It's a very different tax regime for a corporation versus a partnership. I've seen an estimate that, in 2023, if the big four were corporations, they would have contributed around a billion dollars in additional tax to the Commonwealth and states in that year alone. That is in the form of corporate tax, and, for example, payroll tax. What's the public interest in leaving these large commercial enterprises as partnerships when we pay such a price in terms of tax receipts?

Mr J Kelly : Notwithstanding the way you phrased the last end of that question, it's very much a question about tax settings for these firms and large partnerships, so I direct you to the revenue group that are scheduled to appear at 8 pm tonight.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: You think that belongs to the revenue group. I will do that. I'm sure you're aware that the big four operate with the benefit of limited liability via the Professional Standards Act, which provides firm-wide liability caps and insurance, reducing damages to a maximum of around $1,000 a partner by the time it's all boiled down across a partnership—that is, they are doing millions of dollars of consulting work and of course audit work as well, but mostly consulting work, with the possibility of only a damage liability of $1,000. Are you concerned, in Treasury and in this division, that the combination of the big four's avoidance and exclusion from the 20-partner cap in corporations law and their limited liability, by that Professional Standards Act, lets them operate as de facto corporations that are untaxed and unaccountable and very difficult to sue when they go off the rails?

Mr J Kelly : As the minister and other people have said today, we're very concerned about some of the behaviours of these firms. I would have to take it on notice whether we've done any specific work on the Professional Standards Council. That's a good question, so we'll take that on notice.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you. For me it's a competition question. Many, many small consultancy firms do not have the protection of that form of liability protection. That liability protection flows well beyond the 20 per cent of the audit business to all of the consultancy work, and that is an extremely unfair way of treating the system, so I would really like to hear your opinion on that. You say you don't have any work on that under way at present?

Mr Quinlivan : We will have to take it on notice.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you. Finally, I want to come to whistleblower protections. The FOI revealed a table in relation to the main provisions in this report and the way in which the consulting opinions varied across a range of diverse organisations. I'm sure you know it well. The one area on which there was absolutely no disagreement was around whistleblower protection. Now, we're talking about something which is two years old. There was widespread agreement of the fact that partnerships are not required to have any whistleblower protections at the level, say, of corporations, imperfect as they are as well. We know the story of TAHE in New South Wales, where Brendan Lyon paid a huge price for calling out the appalling behaviour that he witnessed. Why no action, Minister or whoever wants to answer?

Mr Quinlivan : The Treasurer has been undertaking a statutory review of the tax and corporate whistleblowing frameworks. We've been doing that for some time, and we've released a consultation paper this week.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Yes. I just waved it. I've read it.

Mr Quinlivan : I appreciate that, Senator. We've opened consultation for eight weeks, till towards the end of July, and we are seeking feedback on a range of these issues. The paper does describe the gap that we have with partnerships and that there are different entities covered between the tax framework, which is based on the topic of tax, and the corporate whistleblowing framework, which only covers entities covered by the Corporations Act. We appreciate that there's a gap there for partnerships on the kinds of issues that might come up in the corporate framework, and we expect the review will flesh those out and go to those.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I'm expressing real frustration that we already have all of the evidence relating to whistleblowing in these large consulting firms. We already have wide support for action on this. This is a review of the broader application of whistleblowing provisions, well beyond consulting. To anyone who put in a submission earlier to the inquiry into changes of behaviour in consulting, you invite them just to resubmit. Why has there been no action in relation to these big four? Mr Quinlivan : I understand. I think the paper invites people to submit, or we'll take that previous information that they've provided. Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Can you tell me what the next steps are. Here's the paper; when do we expect there to be a subsequent set of options, for example?

Mr Quinlivan : There's a consultation process as part of the review. We expect to then provide a review to government. Then it's a matter for government as to taking those recommendations on.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: How long is this period open for?

Mr Quinlivan : The consultation paper process is open for eight weeks.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Minister, can you give us an indication—we're still waiting, two years down the track, for anything in relation to the previous review. Are we going to see something a bit sooner than that, do you think?

Senator CHANDLER: Thanks to the officials from Fiscal Group for coming in this evening. I have some questions around savings measures in the budget. The budget reflects specifically an NDIS related savings measure. Could officials confirm the total net impact of all NDIS related decisions in this budget across the forward estimates.

Mr Donovan : Those figures can be found on page 35 of Budget Paper No. 1, where it says:

These reforms are expected to reduce growth in NDIS payments by $37.8 billion …

That's the gross save figure. There's further information about that save in Budget Paper No. 2, page 106, where it details that measure and also goes through a spend of $1.7 billion over five years in order to implement that measure.

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry, I was jumping around the budget papers while you were saying that. That headline figure for the NDIS related saves is—

Mr Donovan : It's $37.8 billion.

Senator CHANDLER: Wonderful. In the 2024-25 budget, the government also booked a very large NDIS save. I think it was about $14 billion over the forward estimates, with the assertion being, in that budget, that it would take steps to reduce the growth rate of NDIS spending to eight per cent per annum. What was NDIS actual spending growth in 2024-25, and is the government on track to achieve that eight per cent growth or less this financial year?

Senator Gallagher: I think we did go through this a bit last week. We brought spending on the NDIS growth rate down from about 22 per cent to just over 10. The latest actuarial assessment has required us to have an upwards variation of that because the changes that we had sought have not been implemented in a way that has delivered the expected growth—getting that growth down to eight and then below. That's why we've taken further decisions in this budget, including to provide legislative powers for the changes that we need to bring in to bring growth in that scheme down towards five per cent. I'm sure we can provide some more details on that. I think we did traverse this quite extensively in Finance, so I don't think it'll be any—

Senator CHANDLER: We did. I promise not to be so extensive on this at any given time.

Senator Gallagher: Well, it won't be any different to the evidence you heard.

Senator CHANDLER: Mr Donovan, did you have some further details on that question for me?

Mr Donovan : It was just to confirm what the finance minister said, which was that, in 2024-25, the growth rate in the NDIS was just north of 10 per cent; I have it at 10.8 per cent in that year, tracking down from 22.9 per cent in 2022-23.

Senator CHANDLER: So it's fair to say that, prior to the latest new savings measure as part of this budget, the government wasn't on track to achieve the $14 billion saves it had previously booked?

Senator Gallagher: We have achieved a slowing of the growth, and that has had some positive impact on the budget in previous budget years. Some of the ongoing reductions in growth were about getting plan inflation and plan reassessments reduced. At the moment, I think plan inflation is on average around 20 per cent, so it was driving that growth down. The latest actuarial assessment provided to the government shows that that was not on track to be met for a range of reasons, including some decisions of the Federal Court. This budget outlines further adjustments to the NDIS scheme, backed up by legislative powers, to require it by legislation to help us drive down the costs. This is in the first legislation. Obviously, there'll be a second piece of legislation that goes to deal with some of the other matters around eligibility for the scheme in an ongoing sense.

Senator CHANDLER: The saves weren't on track to be achieved previously. Thank you for confirming that, Minister.

Senator Gallagher: Well, we can go back and show you, because it wasn't just $14 billion. I think, over time, there have been other adjustments. We can go back in time, but essentially we've got it down from 22 per cent to 10 per cent. That has been a very significant reduction in expected expenditure.

Senator CHANDLER: But you want it to get to eight per cent.

Senator Gallagher: Yes, but to get to eight from 22 you have to pass through 10, right?

Senator CHANDLER: Yes.

Senator Gallagher: So that's what we're doing. Now, based on the new information we've got about some of the, I think, matters in the courts and some ways that the agency hasn't been able to get plan inflation lower to deliver that eight per cent, we're taking further steps.

Senator CHANDLER: Okay. I might move on quickly to another topic, and we'll see if we can get this done as effectively as possible. I want to turn to page 435 of BP 1. It is, I have to say, one of my least favourite pages in the budget papers because it relates to the government debt bomb. Has the dollar level of gross debt risen each and every year for the past four years?

Senator CHANDLER: I didn't ask about forecasting, Minister. I asked what's in black and white here in the budget papers.

Senator Gallagher: Well, you can read. You can see. Again, we're not going to do your work for you. Everything is published. The point I made on debt last week and I'll continue to make is that it's a lot lower under us than what we inherited. We have been paying it down. We've been paying down interest on that debt. We've been managing the budget responsibly. Based on the commitments that you've made since being returned to opposition, we know that you have no way of delivering on those commitments without increasing debt, increasing deficits and increasing the interest on that debt. Senator CHANDLER: Can the officials assist me here? Is debt going up, yes or no?

Senator Gallagher: You can see what's published in the documents, Senator Chandler. They are there in the table.

Senator CHANDLER: So debt is going up then, isn't it, Minister? That's what's published in the table.

Senator Gallagher: We can go around and we can do this again. Debt is lower in every year compared to what we inherited when we came to government. Under us, debt remains below that level, and because of the decisions we've taken—$176 billion less debt—we have saved around $70 billion in interest costs over the medium term. The point I'm trying to make here is, if you are concerned about gross debt now, you must have been absolutely beside yourself in 2022-23. The position now is much better than the one we inherited.

But it will need continual management, and that is what we've committed to since coming to government, and you'll continue to see it in future budgets as well.

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry, I'm just looking through my questions, trying to figure out if we can possibly get close to the bottom of this. Is net debt as a share of the economy higher at the end of the forwards than it is at the start?

Senator Gallagher: When we came to government, net debt was—

Senator CHANDLER: The wasn't the question.

Senator Gallagher: What you would like is to just completely erase anything that happened under your government and only come in—

Senator CHANDLER: Like the pandemic?

Senator CHANDLER: My question was specifically whether net debt as a share of the economy was higher at the end of the forwards than at the start.

Senator Gallagher: We're going to have to continue to manage the debt, as any government would have to, particularly when they've inherited debt forecasts in the order of $1 trillion of debt, which is what we inherited from you. We're going to have to continue to manage it, and we will. You look at all of the decisions we've taken, every budget; where we can, we return upward revisions of revenue back to the budget, we lower debt, and we lower interest on that debt. And that's partly why the biggest thing you could do if you want to manage the risks on that side of the budget is support the changes to the NDIS, because you can see from the budget papers that the single biggest thing that we can do to manage the pressure on that side of the budget is rein the growth in the NDIS.

CHAIR: You're at 12 minutes.

Senator CHANDLER: I want to start off by getting an understanding and stepping out some of the economic rationale behind the CGT changes in the budget. The government has stated that its objective in this budget is to align the tax rates paid on labour and capital income—and I think the secretary of the department, who appeared this morning, reiterated that in her speech last week. Is that correct, Ms Brown?

Ms D Brown : The tax package message would have had a range of objectives. There is a closer alignment of the tax rates paid on capital and labour, but it also had the general objectives of dealing with intergenerational equity, improving housing outcomes and making a more efficient tax system by removing distortions.

Senator CHANDLER: I'm sure we'll get to those other objectives later this evening. I just want to focus on the labour-capital issue right now. Just to step us back through a bit of history: the Henry tax review was commissioned by a Labor government and developed by Treasury under former secretary Henry. It stated about taxing income from savings:

Comprehensive income taxation, under which all savings income is taxed the same as labour income, is not an appropriate policy goal or benchmark.

That review went on to note that there are reasons beyond inflation to tax the incomes from savings at a lower rate than labour income. I think that former secretary Henry has reindorsed that position recently.

It was also stated in the Mirrlees review, which was a major tax review conducted in the UK, that economic theory provides no compelling reason for why capital income should be taxed at the same rate as labour income and that the capital income tax rate should be well below the top marginal tax rate on labour income. It then went on to give various reasons for this beyond inflation, including international mobility of capital and the difficulties of enforcing taxes on foreign income et cetera. Given that there has been significant literature which has examined this issue previously—and I don't think that it's crazy economics I'm referencing here; it's pretty orthodox—is it appropriate to tax capital income at a substantially lower rate than labour income?

Ms D Brown : I might say a few words and then Dr Johnson may say more. Capital and labour are still being taxed at different rates. Labour will be taxed on nominal income and capital on real income. Labour is taxed on receipt and capital gains are taxed on realisation, and that has a deferral benefit. So there is still a differential within the system between capital and labour income. There are also questions around the relevance of a broad-based tax arrangement to encourage investment in capital—that might be something that you're coming to—because the tax system has a range of other concessions that benefit capital and lead to lower rates across the capital tax system.

As to your questions on the literature, I might see whether Dr Johnson has something he'd like to add.

Dr Johnson : The reforms themselves don't align the tax rates between labour and capital gains. They do move them closer. Capital gains would still be taxed favourably. As Ms Brown mentioned, the existing CGT discount will be replaced with a discount based on the inflationary component of the return through the indexation of the cost base. This direction is consistent with the Henry tax review. The Henry tax review suggested moving to a 40 per cent discount, noting that it actually represents a more realistic inflation adjustment than the 50 per cent discount. This actually goes even a step further and does apply an appropriate adjustment for inflation.

In addition, and as Ms Brown mentioned, capital gains, unlike other forms of income, also benefit from deferral. This will actually reduce the real effective tax rate over time. This is because taxpayers can actually choose when they realise the asset and pay their tax, and so they get a benefit. Essentially, it's like an interest-free loan on the tax liability. In contrast, as Ms Brown mentioned, labour income and other forms of savings are taxed on receipt, with capital gains being taxed on realisation. As I said, that will actually reduce the tax rate. So, while the rates are moving closer together, they're not going towards alignment, and I think they are broadly in line with the principles behind the Henry tax review, which did suggest moving to the 40 per cent discount because it was a better approximation of inflation. A better approximation of inflation than a discount would actually be to adjust for inflation directly.

In addition, I should mention that, if you look at the arrangements as a whole, there are also still favourable taxation arrangements for small business because those small-business tax concessions remain as well. So, if you look at the effective tax rates on those types of investment, again, they're much lower than on labour income.

Senator CHANDLER: Would you agree that there are good economic reasons other than inflation to tax savings less than capital income?

Dr Johnson : If you have a look through history, through the 1970s, the literature went through and looked at the optimal taxation of savings and suggested that the optimal rate is potentially zero. I think that, since that time, research and literature have evolved and highlighted that there is a reason—there are many good reasons—for the taxation of savings. There may be a differential in the rates between labour income and savings, like we've got in this situation. But, yes, certainly there is a good rationale for having some form or level of taxation on savings.

Another thing to also be considering when we are looking at the appropriate rates is the ability to substitute income from one form to another—for example, the ability to substitute labour income into a capital gain. To the extent that is possible and easy to do, again, that would also justify a higher rate, or a positive rate, on savings or on capital gains.

Senator CHANDLER: Isn't it a pretty basic tax principle, though, that capital income taxes are a form of double taxation—that is, individuals are saving out of post-tax income and then investing in something and then having to pay a capital gains tax when they dispose of that investment, which means you've already paid tax on your savings and therefore any returns generated by your savings? The proposed approach to losses, like you mentioned, is that's the same approach that applied for over 15 years when capital gains were first introduced in Australia. That was at a time as well when inflation was higher, and so the impacts are probably sensitive to inflation. One of the reasons behind that is that it's a trade-off. Tax reform and tax policy is always to do with trade-offs. There are trade-offs between efficiency, equity and simplicity to ensure the integrity of the system, and the rationale for using nominal losses is to preserve that integrity of the tax system. That's consistent with other countries that have adopted similar arrangements on the taxation of real gains.

One of the challenges with a realisation based system is that the individual gets to choose when the tax is paid or when a gain or a loss is actually crystallised. They can sell the asset when it's in a loss position, offset it against the gain somewhere else, and then purchase the asset back straightaway. That can actually lead to deferral of tax liability for some time. So it's a choice between what might be a theoretically optimal system and a system that preserves the integrity of the system. In addition, because we do have choice on realisation, it can also affect the portfolio choice. Moving to a system that does have real gains can also affect the portfolio choice of the individual as well. In terms of where this been done before, the UK did temporarily allow real losses to be deductible, but they reversed their approach largely reflecting integrity concerns.

Dr Johnson : We think that around 90 per cent of small businesses would be eligible for the small-business CGT concessions based on the turnover tests.

Senator CHANDLER: That didn't answer my question though. Won't the fact that small businesses have to rely on getting these concessions disincentivise them growing their businesses?

Senator Gallagher: I think there are probably a range of factors around decisions small businesses make. I would think the vast majority of small businesses would want to grow their business, Senator Chandler.

Senator CHANDLER:   I'd like to think so too, but I'm not convinced they do under these changes.

Senator Gallagher: I don't believe reforms to CGT would prevent a small business wanting to grow.

Senator CHANDLER: I don't think that's what the small-business community is saying at the moment, Minister.

Senator Gallagher: We have a range of concessions available. The government also indicated in the budget papers on budget night that we wanted to engage with businesses on the implementation of this and about some of the impacts of this in a range of different ways, and we are doing just that. And we will continue to do that.

Senator CHANDLER: Okay. Higher-productivity businesses are going to get taxed more, aren't they? In contrast to the existing flat discount, any part of the return above inflation is going to be taxed at the full marginal tax rate. That means the higher the return, the higher the effective tax rate. Is that correct?

Dr Johnson : Even a high-productivity business that is eligible for the small business concessions will also have the opportunity to have their capital gains exempt or taxed at 50 per cent. There are two exemption categories and a 50 per cent discount category as well. Higher-productivity—

Senator CHANDLER: What if they aren't eligible for those concessions, though? Let's just remember for the moment that we're talking about bigger—

Dr Johnson : That would depend on the particular circumstances of the business—how much is being reinvested and if it's being invested into the business. That would adjust the cost base and a range of other factors.

Senator CHANDLER: Relative to the existing system, though, that's going to place a greater tax burden on more productive investments and a lower tax burden on less productive investments. Is that correct?

Dr Johnson : No, that's not necessarily correct. It provides a more neutral treatment in relation to the real return, which is important for investment decisions. The current arrangements incentivise more speculative-type investments—investments that may not actually link to the fundamentals. That's one of the reasons for looking at this type of change. The current discount based approach overcompensates some types of investment and undercompensates others. That tends to promote investments in more speculative-type behaviours as opposed to the basic fundamentals.

Senator CHANDLER: The definition of what a small business is isn't consistent across government—that's correct, isn't it?

Dr Johnson : That's correct.

Senator CHANDLER: Can we actually say if there is one consistent way of figuring out exactly how many small businesses are going to have to utilise these exemptions—and I use that term loosely, not in relation to any of the many definitions of small business?

Senator Gallagher: Sorry, what's your question?

Senator CHANDLER: We can't say that all small businesses are eligible for these exemptions, can we, because what a small business is varies?

Senator Gallagher: That's right. We have been clear: the definition for the small business concessions would cover, as I understand it, about 91½ per cent of Australia's 2.7 million businesses.

Senator CHANDLER: How do you get to that 91 per cent? And it's based on what definition of small business?

Senator Gallagher: Businesses with an aggregated annual turnover of less than $2 million or assets with a net value of less than $6 million can access the capital gains tax concessions. And as of June 2025, I'm advised that of the approximately 2.7 million businesses, roughly 8½ per cent would not be covered by the existing small business CGT concessions, based on turnover. That's how I get to that.

Senator CHANDLER: Okay. I want to go back to the 47 per cent for a second. It will not shock you to know that I didn't make that number up: I've seen it consistently in my social media feed since budget night. There is an amusing meme going around, showing the Prime Minister as—

Senator Gallagher: Yes, but it isn't accurate, is it?

Senator CHANDLER: Have you asked Treasury for advice on whether it's accurate, Minister?

Senator Gallagher: I think that the meme is based on—

Senator CHANDLER: I tried to get an answer from you this morning and I didn't.

Senator Gallagher: As I understand it, some of that is based on misinformation: that we are removing the CGT discount. We are not doing that, we are reforming it.

Senator CHANDLER: Have you asked Treasury to do any modelling on whether the 47 per cent is accurate?

Ms D Brown : It isn't accurate, Senator.

Senator CHANDLER: I just have a few more questions on CGT. The government has claimed that CGT changes must be applied to all assets because carving out housing would create a distortion, and that was claimed to be on the basis of Treasury advice. What was that advice?

Dr Johnson : The application to all assets comes from a number of factors. First of all, there is limited justification for having different regimes applying across different asset classes where possible. You may want to have some separate arrangements where you can identify that there might be some positive externality or some positive spillover, and you might want to have some type of arrangement to support that. I think the government have indicated that they will consult with startups and others. That was in the budget. But there's limited rationale to have a broad based discount; we've shown that in budget statement 4. Then there's also limited rationale to have different arrangements across broad asset classes as well. That will also tend to distort investment or savings behaviour. In addition, having different arrangements across different types of asset classes can create significant opportunities for tax arbitrage and restructuring to try and get around other intents of the policy. So moving towards a comprehensive approach makes sense on an efficiency basis and also on a tax system integrity basis.

Senator CHANDLER: Sure. But, if that's the case, Dr Johnson, then why are we carving houses out with the negative gearing changes—

Senator Gallagher: For new builds.

Senator CHANDLER: and not on other assets?

Dr Johnson : Do you mean for new builds?

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry—why are we applying them to one asset type and not the other? That's what I'm getting at.

Dr Johnson : Like I mentioned, sometimes there might be rationales where there is positive spillover or positive benefit, and the government has indicated that having investment in new builds is important and has ensured that they can continue with the existing treatment.

Senator Gallagher: That is to incentivise new supply.

Ms D Brown : Senator, I might draw your attention to other measures in the budget that also have that same effect of creating a distortion for an intended purpose. The changes to the losses reforms that the government is doing are to support small businesses and slightly larger businesses with innovation. The changes to R&D tax incentives are about encouraging R&D, but that means someone is getting a bigger deduction than they otherwise would be. So there are a range of measures that might have those exemptions, but you do it in a very targeted and considered way, which means that you're minimising the distortion that it is creating.

Senator CHANDLER: But you can negatively gear shares, can't you? You can borrow to buy that asset.

Dr Johnson : You can. Currently, I think, about 98 per cent of negative gearing relates to property.

Senator Gallagher: Established property.

Senator CHANDLER: I'm just asking about the principle, though. Why can shares continue to be negatively geared but existing houses can't?

Dr Johnson : Like I said, the majority of negative gearing takes place through property. When we look at the distortions that come about from the existing system, a large part is in relation to the application of the capital gains tax discount. As a proxy for inflation, it doesn't quite do the job. Removing that and replacing it with indexation moves us to an arrangement where it's more likely that decisions will be based on the underlying economics of the investment as opposed to tax preferences. Negative gearing is a smaller issue in relation to shares. There are very few people—I think about two per cent of negative gearing comes from things outside of property, so it's a much, much smaller problem.

Senator CHANDLER: Just one more question, Chair—I'll flip that around for you then, Dr Johnson: if it's such a good idea, why couldn't you carve out shares from the CGT changes as well?

Dr Johnson : What would be the rationale for carving shares out of the CGT changes?

Senator CHANDLER: Well, that would be a question for you.

Dr Johnson : I think I answered that before, when I indicated that it's important to have neutrality across asset classes in your tax system. If we don't do that, then we're going to have—it relates to two issues. You're going to have a bias towards investing through particular types of investments and, that way, you're going to distort the asset allocation. Alternatively, it really does put pressure on tax minimisation and arbitrage. Individuals will restructure to benefit from tax concessions. We see it frequently throughout the tax system. I think, on two cases, having a more uniform, consistent approach across assets supports better economic—

Senator CHANDLER: But it's not consistent.

Dr Johnson : But it is. The CGT arrangements are consistent.

Senator CHANDLER: Not with the negative gearing changes, they're not.

Dr Johnson : The negative gearing changes—like I said, very few people use negative gearing for shares.

Senator Gallagher: It's 98 per cent in established property.

Ms D Brown : There are features of negative gearing of share that make it less attractive than negative gearing of property, usually—

Senator CHANDLER: Less attractive?

Ms D Brown : less attractive—because the security is not as good as the security of a house. The banks will also charge more interest.

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry, you mean less attractive as an investment option. Thank you, Chair.

CHAIR: Senator Bell.

Senator BELL: I've got some questions about the CGT changes as well, specifically about whether everyday Australians can be reasonably expected to comply with the new laws without needing a tax agent or paying for software or a forensic reconstruction of every dividend reinvestment parcel they have accumulated over 10, 15 or 20 years. A taxpayer with a dividend reinvestment plan doesn't just own one parcel of shares. Every reinvestment dividend can create another acquisition parcel, so over time a modest portfolio can become hundreds of separate records. I think Australians deserve to know whether this matter was modelled—whether Treasury looked at the paperwork burden, whether the ATO is able to administer it simply and if the government actually understands what it might cost everyday investors to comply. The question I have first is: did the Treasury model the additional compliance burden on individual taxpayers of replacing the 50 per cent CGT discount with a cost based indexation?

Ms D Brown : The department did prepare an impact assessment, and, as part of that, you do look at the compliance costs. That impact assessment is published on the Office of Impact Analysis website, and that does show that there is a limited compliance cost associated with the changes.

Senator BELL: And what is that compliance cost?

Ms D Brown : That compliance cost is a total—$88.4 million average annual regulatory costs.

Senator BELL: For a taxpayer holding 20 listed shares, with two dividend reinvestments per year over 15 years, how many calculations would that taxpayer need to perform?

Ms D Brown : It would depend on how often they realised the asset. Capital gains is only applicable when you realise the share.

Senator BELL: I beg your pardon; I'm having trouble hearing you.

Ms D Brown : It depends on how often they trade in the shares, because capital gains is only liable upon realisation of the shares. People will hold shares and not trade for long periods of time.

Senator BELL: What if they decided to realise them all?

Dr Johnson : Under the current arrangements, you need to keep track of your cost base for your assets so you can work out your capital gain, and that does not change.

Senator BELL: Under the new system, if a taxpayer realised all of those shares, they're not going to be required to make any additional calculations?

Dr Johnson : No. They will still need to understand their original cost base and their sale price. The difference here is then you will make a calculation to provide an uplift from the cost base, for inflation. To be able to do that, the ATO will have software or have tools and things available to make it easier.

Senator BELL: So, using that example of 20 listed shares and two dividend reinvestments per 15 years, if they decide to realise them all at the same time, how many calculations are they likely to need to perform?

Dr Johnson : It's the same number of calculations as now because they still need to—

Senator BELL: What would that be?

Dr Johnson : I'm not sure, sorry.

Senator Gallagher: I don't know that Treasury can do this on the spot, based on a scenario that's just given to them. What they're saying is that they're the same arrangements that exist now.

Senator BELL: So could you take on notice my question on that scenario?

Dr Johnson : Yes, sure.

Senator BELL: Under the original system, under that scenario and then under the proposed changes—could you provide the answers to those on notice?

Dr Johnson : Yes.

Senator BELL: Thank you. On the modelling and impact statement you've provided, did the Treasury provide to the government the cost of compliance of this reform, including additional accountant fees and tax software costs, that are likely to be incurred?

Ms D Brown : The compliance costs consider a range of factors. They included the costs both to the taxpayer as well as to their adviser. That's the cost to their adviser in learning about the new skills and advising their clients, the new recordkeeping they might need to do and the new procedures they might need to put in place.

Senator BELL: What was the cost of that?

Ms D Brown : I've only got an aggregate number available to me tonight.

Senator BELL: And what is that aggregate number?

Ms D Brown : That was the $88.4 million.

Senator BELL: Is that the same one? Okay. Did the Treasury advise the government that this reform could increase compliance costs for investors? If so, was that advice provided before the policy was announced?

Ms D Brown : It's ordinarily to provide this type of advice as part of budget processes.

Senator Gallagher: Yes. The government was well briefed by Treasury before we made these decisions. And, in addition to the ones that you're raising, the budget also has a range of tax simplification reforms, including instant deduction, instant asset write-off, removing nuisance tariffs and reducing compliance costs. You have to see it in totality with a whole range of other measures that the government has agreed with.

Senator BELL: Alright. In relation to the ATO—under the proposed system, will a taxpayer need to calculate an indexed cost base for each relevant acquisition parcel? In the case of dividend reinvestment plans, will each reinvested dividend generally create a separate acquisition parcel? Do we know?

Mr Heferen : The final shape of the legislation and what's actually going to be required are yet to be determined. Until such time as we see the specifics of whether the parliament ends up with the legislation, it's probably unwise to speculate in the meantime. Also, given the inherent uncertainties that might at the moment be the case, we're not sure what shape the final legislation will take.

Senator BELL: What are those inherent uncertainties?

Mr Heferen : The parliament might make some amendment to what's currently being proposed. And so, in the ATO, we always try to be constructive. We obviously work with our colleagues and the Treasury to provide as much in-time advice as we can to assist them in their policy deliberations and advice to the government. But, when it comes to providing a view here, that could be then taken out of context. So the Commissioner has said that this will be the case, but, until such time as the legislation is final, us providing what could be taken as definitive advice would be a bit premature.

Senator BELL: So you can't say whether you'll require taxpayers to maintain or reconstruct parcel-level records.

Mr Heferen : Taxpayers will have to keep records—

Senator Gallagher: Like they do now.

Mr Heferen : As Dr Johnson said before, the requirements now to keep records to establish what the capital gain might be when that asset is realised—that principle stays the same. At the moment, people need to keep records about the value of their asset, and, upon realisation, work out the capital gain. Of course, bear in mind that this a self-assessment system, so they're the ones doing it. If the way the capital gain is to be taxed changes, which is what the proposal is, then the principle about what records they need to keep remains the same. What will change is the resulting tax that would be payable.

Senator BELL: As you model, there'll be an additional compliance cost for individuals. It's likely to become more complex for them.

Mr Heferen : Well, I don't necessarily understand why. And, as I think Ms Brown said, we at the Tax Office will work closely with agents, the digital service providers and, of course, our own staff to make sure there are guidance, materials and tools for taxpayers who are going to do this themselves, and not through an agent, to make the task of complying with the legislation as straightforward and low-cost as possible. That's what we aim to do across all areas of tax, but particularly those where it's more likely used by an individual or a small business, who, in the scheme of things, are usually less able to afford the external advice. We'll attempt to make sure that is as smooth, seamless and clear as possible.

Senator BELL: Have you already begun developing those free tools?

Mr Heferen : In the discussion with our colleagues in the Treasury, we're certainly scoping out what things might look like. But, as I say, a lot will depend on the final shape.

Senator Gallagher: The legislation.

Senator BELL: You've already looked at what some of these tools might look like.

Mr Heferen : Well, without wanting to pretend they are going to be new tools, we actually have a whole range of tools. I think sometimes the common term is 'artefact'. That's not a thing that you dig out of a cave but things that people can use to assist them in understanding their obligations and their payment.

Senator BELL: Can you guarantee that an individual, everyday investor with a long-running DRP would be able to comply accurately without having to pay for tax software or additional accounting fees?

Mr Heferen : Guarantees about the future are probably a fraction unwise. I think the future is inherently uncertain., so I wouldn't like to have a guarantee here, and people find in the future there's one particular circumstance where someone had to do something different to what they'd otherwise do. I wouldn't like to be in a position of trying to guarantee. But I can give the committee assurance that we will do everything we can to ensure that in the legislation, when it's passed, the obligations on taxpayers will be as clearly understood and as straightforward as we're able to make.

Senator BELL: It does sound like you believe it will impose an increased private compliance cost on taxpayers.

CHAIR: Senator, I'm going to have to rotate the call, if you can finish.

Mr Heferen : As Dr Johnson said before, on the question about the increase, we'll have to just see how it works through. What an individual taxpayer will have to do in terms of keeping information and then establishing what needs to be paid upon realisation of the asset—that work needs to be done now. I think what we're talking about is the amount of tax that's going to be paid, rather than the recordkeeping of the assets' value.

CHAIR: Senator Chandler.

Senator CHANDLER: I'll go back to the CGT, we'll do a quick few more on negative gearing, and then I think I'll be done for the evening. Won't the minimum 30 per cent tax rate hit the lowest income Australians the hardest?

Ms D Brown : In the tax explainer, I'll just try and find that. We do talk about exemptions for certain income recipients.

Senator CHANDLER: I know there are exemptions for people receiving welfare. That's correct?

Senator Gallagher: On payments—yes.

Dr Johnson : Yes, that's right. For individuals on payments, the minimum 30 per cent wouldn't apply. As we outlined in budget statement 4, we looked at 2022-23, and around 95 per cent of net capital gains were earned by individuals who either wouldn't be affected by the minimum tax or who would have had a marginal tax rate of more than 30 per cent during their working lives.

Senator CHANDLER: What about self-funded retirees or Australians taking time out of the workforce? Women on maternity leave come to mind. Aren't they going to be worse off?

Dr Johnson : It would depend on their individual circumstances.

Senator CHANDLER: But they're still going to have to pay the 30 per cent minimum, aren't they?

Senator Gallagher: In the situation where they realise a gain—is this what you're saying?

Senator CHANDLER: Yes.

Senator Gallagher: Well, you just heard evidence that, for the overwhelming majority of taxpayers, 95 per cent—

Dr Johnson : Of capital gains.

Senator Gallagher: in terms of capital gains would not be—sorry, I don't want to verbal Dr Johnson.

Dr Johnson : Around 95 per cent of capital gains would have been earned by people who are not affected by the minimum tax—for example, they are on income support or they're already facing marginal tax rates that are at 30 per cent or above or they would have faced a marginal tax rate of at least 30 per cent through their working life.

Senator CHANDLER: So anyone receiving a welfare payment—

Dr Johnson : Income support.

Senator CHANDLER: you say, is carved out. They are going to be paying less CGT than someone who's earning less income than them but without a welfare payment. That doesn't seem quite fair.

Dr Johnson : When we looked at individuals, a lot of those individuals who would be subject to the 30 per cent rate were individuals who were higher-income individuals during their working lives. What this aims to do is to try and reduce incentives to hold on to assets for too long to wait until you are facing lower tax rates.

Senator CHANDLER: Sorry, I don't know if that answered my question. I thought it was more straightforward than that. If you're on a welfare payment you are carved out, so you won't have to pay the minimum 30 per cent tax rate if you realise a capital gain, but a self-funded retiree or someone taking time out from the workforce is going to get hit with the 30 per cent.

Dr Johnson : It would depend on their circumstances.

Senator Gallagher: It's very difficult to give individual tax advice on hypothetical situations that don't bring all of the information to the table. It is impossible for Treasury to sit here and—

Senator CHANDLER: I wouldn't have thought they were that hypothetical.

Senator Gallagher: say someone who might be a self-funded retiree, without knowing anything else about the situation they're in or the decisions that they've taken or the assets they're disposing of—it's ridiculous.

Senator CHANDLER: These aren't completely obsolete groups of Australians that I'm talking about. I would have thought Treasury would have done some sort of analysis on the impact on these kinds of groups.

Senator Gallagher: They have and they're explaining that to you.

Senator CHANDLER: But they can't—

Senator Gallagher: They can't give individual advice on an individual, hypothetical situation that has half or less than half the information—that is, a self-funded retiree and nothing else. They cannot give advice on that.

Senator CHANDLER: I would have thought these were pretty straightforward questions, but I'll persevere. The negative-gearing changes have been purported to improve the efficiency of the housing market, but what impact do the grandfathering provisions have on that? I would have thought that would have more of a lock-in effect than anything else.

Senator Gallagher: I think the secretary went through this earlier today in a question from Senator McKim—it might have been the secretary, I think, when you asked about the turnover—and her advice was that, I think, in most situations a property moves from negative gearing to positive gearing within six to seven years. That's outlined in the budget papers. We believe this is the right decision to take. Already, over the last couple of weekends since the budget, I think we have been seeing promising signs of first home buyers being able to compete to purchase a property not necessarily outbid by investors.

Senator CHANDLER: Has there been any analysis on whether people who are grandfathered will be keeping their houses rather than turning them over to the market?

Senator Gallagher: I think the evidence is, again, that they shift from being negatively geared to being positively geared, so some of the benefits that come with being negatively geared are lost over time. The government has taken a decision, in terms of our tax reform, that investment decisions made prior to budget night are protected by the decisions we've made. We think that that was the right decision. That has resulted in grandfathering arrangements for those who have investments that operated before budget night. For those that operate before budget night on 1 July 2027, negative gearing applies for that year, for that period, before the new arrangements kick in, subject to legislation passing, of course.

Senator CHANDLER: With the exemption for new houses, do we also run the risk that that disincentivises the selling of them as well? Aren't you concerned this will lock young Australians out of homes?

Senator Gallagher: We think it incentivises investment in new supply, which is something that, as you know, we as a government are very focused on.

Senator CHANDLER: But does it then disincentivise the turnover of those houses?

Senator Gallagher: The same arrangements would apply.

Ms D Brown : I don't think so. One of the roles of the minimum of 30 per cent is to mitigate that lock-in effect, because suddenly their personal income tax rates won't influence when they sell. They can sell and they can buy new supply—a new, new house—and continue that investment and the same CGT treatment with a new build. They can repurchase, from the proceeds, a further new build.

Senator CHANDLER: Is that my time, Chair?

CHAIR: Okay. Senator McKim, I believe you're sharing your 10 minutes with Senator Hodgins-May.

Senator McKIM: I am. I'll kick us off. I want to go back to the discussion on the PRRT that we were having earlier this evening. Firstly, starting with the ATO, just so I'm clear, many companies, for many projects, have never paid PRRT. Some have paid some amounts of PRRT. But when a gas company decommissions a project, if it has paid PRRT on that project, it gets its deductions—the costs of the decommissioning—back from the ATO as a cash payment, capped at the level of PRRT that it's paid; is that right? Is that fair?

Mr Hirschhorn : It's a deduction in the calculation. In a year where it has net deductions and it has previously paid PRRT under that ownership, there is the potential for a refund of previously paid PRRT.

Senator McKIM: As cash?

Mr Hirschhorn : As cash.

Senator McKIM: Yes. Do we pay interest on the loan that they're giving us?

Mr Hirschhorn : We do not pay interest on that loan.

Senator McKIM: We don't? That's what we're talking about here.

Mr Hirschhorn : The tax office is not a bank.

Senator McKIM: It's not so much tax that many gas projects are paying under PRRT arrangements, is it, Minister? It's a short-term loan to the government, because they get it back as cash from the ATO when they decommission their project.

Ms D Brown : Mr Robinson has joined the table. He might be able—

Senator McKIM: That's nice. I was asking the minister because I fear I'm straying into opinion here and I don't think it's fair to ask any of the staff.

Senator Gallagher: Let's have some advice from the experts first.

Ms D Brown : Mr Robinson can elaborate a bit more on the way the PRRT works and the purpose of the decommissioning refund.

Mr Robinson : As Mr Hirschhorn indicated broadly earlier, the reason the decommissioning expenses are generally refunded under the PRRT at the end of the project is that that's the point at which the project has ceased deriving income. But if you look at the life cycle of a project and the various costs that business incurs through the exploration, as well as the construction of infrastructure to support extraction—

Senator McKIM: They're all deductions as well.

Mr Robinson : that's all deductible, as is—

Senator McKIM: With a carry-forward and a very generous uplift provision, I might add.

Mr Robinson : That's right, the point being that it's important that the decommissioning work is undertaken at the end of the project. The end of the project is obviously the point at which things like environmental remediation occur as well, and those are legitimate deductible costs against the PRRT.

The other thing I would add is that, when the entity receives the refund for those decommissioning expenses, that is also treated as income for corporate income tax purposes, so they would actually pay additional tax on the amounts that are being credited.

Senator McKIM: When the budget shows revenue from the PRRT, does that factor in expected decommissioning costs?

Dr Johnson : Yes, it does.

Senator McKIM: Do you have visibility or data on how much PRRT, each project, is expected to pay, or has paid, and what the expected decommissioning cost for each of those projects is?

Dr Johnson : We don't have on a company or project by project—there's a taxpayer confidentiality. We can't provide information on those specific projects. I think the ATO had a response to a question on notice before that talked about publicly available information.

Senator McKIM: Do you have that data though?

Dr Johnson : I'll have to take that on notice and check to see if we have that data.

Senator McKIM: Back to the ATO, how much cash, if any, has the ATO handed back to which companies for which projects and over what timeframes?

Mr Hirschhorn : To expand on Dr Johnson's answer to the previous question, the ATO of course has information on what has happened, whereas we do not do projections of the life cycle of projects. Again, I have referred in the past to the Callaghan review being probably the most complete projection of projects. We do disclose, each year, under the corporate tax transparency measure, the PRRT paid by companies. I'll put a caveat on it and take it on notice, but I think that would also disclose if we gave cash refunds. So to the best of my knowledge at the table—although, I will take it on notice—I do not think we have paid any project a cash refund to date.

Senator McKIM: But you expect to in the future?

Mr Hirschhorn : It is possible, in the last year of a project, as it ceases production and moves into decommissioning—a feature of super profits tax is that it works out the super profit over the life cycle. The government will have overcollected the super profits on the way, and we'll have to then refund the extent to which the super profit has been overstated. So one would expect that at the end of any particular project there will be a little bit of the PRRT paid back.

Senator McKIM: Potentially quite a bit. NOPSEMA estimates $66 billion in decommissioning costs for offshore oil and gas by 2070, with about 55 per cent of that cost being incurred by 2040. We're talking about big bickies here and big costs; therefore, they're potentially big cash refunds.

Senator Gallagher: Presumably, you want these operations decommissioned properly—

Senator McKIM: I'd like the gas companies to actually pay for the gas that they're making eye-watering profits from, Minister. That's what I would like, and my colleagues would like that too.

Senator Gallagher: They don't only pay PRRT, Senator McKim, and presumably—

Senator McKIM: I'm not talking about company tax; everyone pays company tax. I know that's what you were going to say.

Senator Gallagher: Presumably, you would like these operations decommissioned appropriately as well, or do you want the government to pay for that?

Senator McKIM: Of course they should be decommissioned. Treasury said you factored in decommissioning costs when you booked the revenue from PRRT in the budget. Do you rely on the companies' estimations for decommissioning costs, do you conduct your own work, or do you get someone like NOPSEMA to do it? Because the companies, in my view, are grossly underestimating their decommissioning costs in their annual reports because it makes their balance sheets look better.

Dr Johnson : One of the challenges with decommissioning costs is that they are lumpy and they can occur at any time. We have our own assumptions around decommissioning costs that we adopt. We try and provide an accurate reflection on what we think the decommissioning costs would be on average over the forecast horizon.

Senator McKIM: Do what the companies put in their annual reports influence your estimations at all?

Dr Johnson : We will look at a range of sources—

Senator McKIM: Does it include those?

Dr Johnson : We will look at those. We will talk to the department of industry—

Before November last year, we had no engagement. Now the agencies are all on the same page as us, doing everything they can.

Mr Heferen, could you outline exactly what sham contracting is, why it's a concern to the ATO and what you have been doing following Senator Sterle's industry roundtable.

Mr Heferen : With sham contracting, the phrase is often used to refer to a situation where an employer misrepresents the relationship with an employee. They assert to take that person to work for them in a contract arrangement, when, to all intents and purposes, it's actually an employee relationship. I make the point at the outset that the employer-employee relationship is fundamentally a matter for the Fair Work Act and the Fair Work Ombudsman. The Fair Work Ombudsman, if you like, polices those arrangements as to whether employers are trying to get around obligations they might have for employees by effectively renaming them a contractor.

Senator O'NEILL: I might just table the Fair Work Ombudsman statement about this from 13 March for those who want to look this up or are interested as we discuss it. Please go ahead.

Mr Heferen : There's a range of things in an employer-employee relationship, going to having a safe work practice, a range of standards of working hours and so forth that are a matter for industrial awards and the particular employment contract they're working under. That's a matter for the ombudsman.

Where the ATO is interested is that the employer has an obligation to the employee to pay them their wages and withhold an amount and pay it to the ATO so we can put it in the government's bank account and it can be used by the government for public purposes. Also the employer has an obligation to pay the employee superannuation. One of the ways of trying to get around that obligation to pay superannuation would be by saying it's actually a contract and not an employee. So the obligation of employers to make good on their superannuation payments to employees is a matter of great interest to us. We obviously administer the superannuation guarantee system. We make sure that those payments are made and paid in full. Of course, with upcoming payday super, it will be even more important for that to be done in a timely way. Also we want to make sure that the right amount of income tax is withheld from the employee and passed on to us.

Senator O'NEILL: There are other items like leave entitlements and workplace protections that fall under the proper employment relationship rather than sham, meaning pretence, contracting.

Mr Heferen : I would say that whilst, as public servants, we would be concerned about that, that is the remit of the Fair Work Ombudsman. Because of the nature of the interconnectedness of the other elements, in some of these discussions Australian Border Force has been involved because there have been tip-offs provided to the Shadow Economy Taskforce, which we head up, of employers taking people on visas on a contract. There is some concern about whether that arrangement actually contravenes the visa because the visa would typically be an employment one. The tip-off, the allegation, would be where the employer is not actually treating them as an employee consistent with their visa requirements and is actually trying to get them to be a contractor. Border Force is interested from the point of view of the visa requirement; the Fair Work Ombudsman is interested from the sham-contracting point of view; and we're interested from the point of view of making sure the right amount of superannuation is paid to the employee and that the right amount of tax is withheld.

Each of our organisations is subject to quite strict confidentiality provisions. So, prima facie, unless a crime has occurred, we're restricted about what we can share with our colleagues and other agencies, and, likewise, they will be restricted in what they can share. To deal with that under the tax administration act, under section 355, schedule 1, there's the capacity for a minister to establish a taskforce. One of the conditions of the taskforce would be 'a taskforce for a specific purpose', but, in that, the information-sharing can occur. That's what we agencies are doing: we're sharing information to try and make sure our intelligence is put together and coordinated to enable us to be most effective in our compliance activity, so that we don't have one agency looking at one thing, another agency looking at another and another agency looking at another, where, in fact, they're interrelated.

Senator O'NEILL: That's repetition and waste, so there's a productivity benefit—

Mr Heferen : A massive productivity benefit.

Senator O'NEILL: but there's also a community benefit to people who'll find themselves in much more secure employment if this practice is stamped out, because it's very anti-competitive. It's undercutting the market, in many cases, and it's also exploiting workers, who have a right to better conditions.

The Single Touch Payroll is something people hear about but don't always know about. I know that the ATO has referred to an extensive data-matching capability. How does the agency use such a thing as the Single Touch Payroll, ABN records, tax returns and contractor reporting information to identify potential sham-contracting arrangements, in addition to the tip-offs that you've already mentioned?

Mr Heferen : I might get my colleague Mr Hirschhorn to deal with that one.

Mr Hirschhorn : Single Touch Payroll—just to give a bit of context—is the system where, at the point of payment, information is provided to the tax office about the salary that is being paid. That is very useful for where there's actually an employee and where the employer is not pretending that they're anything other than an employee. That data we use routinely for many purposes, but part of it is so that, when you log into your app or myGov—hopefully at the end of July, not on 1 July—at the end of July all of your income is there, and so you don't have to find your old payslip; it's already in your tax return.

Around, let's say, contracting industries—that's for general contractor compliance but also for identifying pretend contractors—the main reporting data that we rely on is called TPRS, which is the taxable payments reporting system. It's generally focused on high-risk industries, which include construction and road freight, coincidentally, where an employer—in the broad sense, somebody who uses a service: say, a road freight service—must report to us the amounts they pay to their contractors or to the people they're saying are contractors. This the primary basis for us to ensure that those contractors don't just pocket the money and not lodge a tax return. So we run a big data-matching program across that, and, indeed, now, increasingly, we're moving that to prefill.

When a contractor—let's say a person who is being characterised as a road freight contractor—lodges their tax return, that reporting will already be in their tax return, the same way it would be if they were a salary earner. That helps us ensure that at least tax is paid. It also ensures that we know that those people are in the system and that they are in an industry, but it doesn't tell us much about whether they're a true contractor or a fake contractor. At this stage, we just know they're being paid as a contractor.

We then, I suppose, use that hard payment data in conjunction with various other information sources—which may be, for example, some visa information or it might be tip-offs—to then identify those purported contractors who might be either true employees or employees within the extended definition for super. We also have information coming from—this is, of course, a very big initiative which is coming in on 1 July, a real game changer—Payday Super, where we will now know in real time if that supposed contractor has had superannuation paid on their behalf. So we will now be able to see which are the contractors, because if there's a contractor who has been reported to us under TPRS, and they are being paid super, we're probably less worried, because their super entitlements are being met. We're making sure we get their tax. This will now be the triangulation of data, which, together with other sources, means we will be able to identify suspicious contractors.

Of course, the nature of the PRRT, again—I think it's really important to go back. It is a superprofits tax over the life of a project. The uplift factors are to try to give a recognition of the superprofit. Obviously, the level of that uplift is a policy matter, but the idea of the uplift is to give a superprofit. The nature of a closing-down expenditure is that it's right at the end of the project, so it gets no uplift because it is used immediately, at the moment that it is effectively expended.
